reveal.text: The same word is used for the piece that connects a web framework to a use case.

lead.text: Ports and adapters are not free. Each port is another interface, each adapter is another file, and the data has to be mapped between the domain's shapes and the outside ones. For a small program that reads a form and writes a row, the structure is more work than the program, and a plain layered design serves better.

It pays where the rules are rich, so that testing them without a database matters, or where the inputs vary, as with one use case driven by a web page, a command line and a schedule. The framework is not the architecture: a web framework is an adapter, and the domain should not need it in order to run.

reveal.text: The fix is for the domain to return its own plain data, and for the web adapter to build the `Response`.

lessons.orientation: Draw the direction of dependencies in layered and hexagonal designs, and recognise an import that breaks the dependency rule.
lessons.nextAction: Compare a modular monolith with microservices, and work out how availability falls as services are chained.

blocks.text: A layered design lets each layer depend only on the layers beneath it, with presentation at the top and the database at the bottom, so that the arrows run one way and are easy to count. They do not show everything, however, because a column called `cust_nm` in the database tends to be copied as `order.cust_nm` in the domain, then as `dto.cust_nm` in the application's data transfer object, a plain record for passing data between layers, and then as a field in the JSON that clients read, and renaming the column then reaches every layer above it.
Ports and adapters repair this by reversing one arrow: the domain states in its own words what it needs, such as a way to store orders, and code on the outside supplies it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count the dependencies a layering allows, say what a port and an adapter are, and spot an import that points the wrong way.

recap.keyIdea: Dependencies should point inward, toward a domain that owns its ports, with adapters for frameworks and databases on the outside.

blocks.text: Layers limit which way dependencies run, but a database at the bottom can still shape every layer above, and ports and adapters repair that by letting the domain own the interface that the database implements. The dependency rule, that imports point inward and never to frameworks, is the check, and the structure is worth its cost where the rules are rich or the inputs vary.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson steps up to whole systems, and compares a modular monolith with microservices.

lessons.title: Monolith, modules and microservices

reveal.text: Mechanisms such as timeouts and retries change this picture, and the System Design course covers them.

lead.text: The same system can take three shapes. A **tangled monolith** is one deployable unit in which anything calls anything, so every change can spread. A **modular monolith** is also one unit, but its code is divided into modules with enforced boundaries, and modules call one another only through interfaces. **Microservices** are independently deployable services, each owning its data and communicating over the network.

Splitting into services buys three things: each service can be deployed on its own, scaled on its own, and owned by a team that does not wait for the others. It costs three things too: every call that crosses the network can fail or be slow, data is spread across services and must be kept consistent between them, and there are many more things to run and watch.

diagram.alt: The same six parts of a shop drawn three ways. A tangled monolith has nine calls between parts in one unit. A modular monolith has five, only between neighbours, in one unit. Microservices have the same five calls, each across a network.

lead.text: If a request must pass through every service in a chain, it succeeds only when all of them are up. When failures are independent, the availability of the chain is the *product* of the availabilities, so five services of 99.9% each give 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999, which is about 0.995.

This is the **distribution cost**. A module call inside a monolith can fail only with the whole program, while a call between services can fail on its own, and a chain of services is less available than any one of them. The size of the fall is easy to underestimate, because each service looks reliable when it is viewed alone.

afterFigure.text: Retries, caches and timeouts can soften the effect. The first question for a style is still how many calls cross the network, and what each one costs.

reveal.text: The product of a long chain falls quickly.

lead.text: In April 1968 Melvin Conway published an observation in *Datamation*, in a paper called "How Do Committees Invent?", that organisations which design systems are constrained to produce designs that copy their own communication structures. The name **Conway's law** came later. Three teams that talk little produce three parts that talk little, and the interfaces between them end up where the teams meet.

If you want four services with clear interfaces, arrange four teams first, each owning one, because a team structure that cuts across the design will drag the design toward itself. This is why the team is part of the question when choosing between a monolith and services, and why a team of six has no need of ten services.

diagram.alt: Two arrangements of teams and services. In one, three teams each own a service, and the services talk where the teams talk. In the other, an organisation that wants four services is first split into four teams, one per service.
diagram.caption: Services tend to follow the teams that build them. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The rule is stated about organisations in general, and it works in both directions: shape the teams to get the design you want.

lead.text: The sensible start for a new system with unclear boundaries is a modular monolith. Boundaries can be moved cheaply while they are still wrong, and a module can be split into a service when something measurable demands it, such as a part that needs to scale alone or a team that is blocked by another.

Two services that read and write the same table are not independent, because the schema of that table can be changed only with the agreement of both, and a change to either service's use of it can break the other. Services get their independence only if each owns its own data and others reach it through its interface.

A service buys independence, so the reason to split should be one that independence solves.

lessons.orientation: Weigh a modular monolith against microservices, work out how availability falls in a chain, and use Conway's law to include the teams in the decision.
lessons.nextAction: Tell commands from events, and say what event sourcing and CQRS add.

blocks.text: A service that is available 99.9% of the time is unavailable for about 43 minutes in a 30-day month, which sounds dependable. A request that has to pass through several such services in turn succeeds only when every one of them is up at the same moment, so the chain is less available than any single service in it, and the more services it has, the further it falls.

That fall is one of the costs of dividing a program into services that talk across a network, and it has to be set against what the division buys, which is independent deployment and teams that do not wait for each other.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to describe three shapes of system, work out the availability of a chain of services, and say why the team structure belongs in the choice.

recap.keyIdea: Services buy independence with network calls and operations, so start from a modular monolith and split on a measurable reason.

blocks.text: Microservices turn module boundaries into network calls, which can fail on their own, so availability multiplies along a chain: five services of 99.9% give 99.5%. Conway's law says that the system will follow the teams that build it, which is why teams are shaped to the architecture wanted, and services that share a database are coupled through its tables.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at how services talk to each other, through commands, events and the patterns built on them.

lessons.title: Events, commands and messages

reveal.text: Storing events and working out the state from them is called event sourcing, and a later screen names it.

lead.text: Messages between services come in two kinds that look alike and behave differently. A **command** asks a service to do something, such as `ReserveStock`. It is addressed to one receiver, and the receiver may refuse it, for example because only two items are left. An **event** records that something *has* happened, such as `OrderPlaced`. It is announced to anyone who is listening, and it cannot be refused, because it is already true.

The names carry the difference. A command is written in the imperative, PlaceOrder or ReserveStock, because it asks. An event is written in the past tense, OrderPlaced or StockReserved, because it reports.

afterFigure.text: Events are not free of coupling. A service that reads OrderPlaced depends on the shape of the event, so the shape is a contract that has to be changed with the care that any public interface needs.

diagram.alt: A command and an event compared. A command such as ReserveStock is sent to one receiver, which may refuse it. An event such as OrderPlaced is announced to anyone who listens, and cannot be refused because it records what has happened.
diagram.caption: A command is a request, and an event is a record. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The same test sorts any message the system sends.

lead.text: An order needs payment, stock and shipping. In **choreography** the services react to one another's events: Orders announces `OrderPlaced`, Payment hears it and announces `PaymentTaken`, Stock hears that and announces `StockReserved`, and Shipping carries on from there. Nobody holds the whole flow, and it is visible only in the events as they pass.

In **orchestration** a coordinator holds it. It sends a command to Payment, waits for the reply, then sends a command to Stock, and so on, so the steps are written in one place and a failure can be handled there. Choreography couples the services loosely and is easy to extend with a new listener. Orchestration is easier to follow and debug, since one place knows what happens next, at the price of a central service that every flow depends on.

afterFigure.text: A flow with a few steps that are unlikely to change suits an orchestrator, while a notification that many parts may want suits an event.

reveal.text: In choreography there is one event per step, and no replies.

lead.text: Most systems store the current state, a balance of 35, and lose how it came to be. **Event sourcing** stores the sequence of events instead, deposit 50, withdraw 20 and deposit 5, and rebuilds the state by **replaying** them from the start.

The log is the record, and the balance is only a way of reading it. This gives a full history for free, and any earlier state can be rebuilt by replaying the log up to that point. It also changes what a mistake looks like: a wrong event is not erased but corrected by a later event, as a ledger entry is corrected with another entry.

afterFigure.text: The cost is that replay applies *every* event it finds, in order. A duplicated or reordered event changes the result, so consumers need to deal with duplicates, with ordering and with the shape of old events, which also change over time.

reveal.text: The log keeps all four events, and the balance is only a way of reading them.

lead.text: A single model has to serve two different jobs. When changing data it must check rules and keep the data consistent, and when reading it must supply whatever each screen needs, perhaps from many records at once. When the two differ a great deal, one model pulls both jobs out of shape. **CQRS**, command query responsibility segregation, separates them: commands go to a write model that guards the rules, and queries go to a read model shaped for the screens.

The two are connected by events. The write model publishes an event for each change, and the read model updates itself from them, so the read model may be a moment behind. This is **eventual consistency**, and it is a property of the design, not a defect: a reader may briefly see the earlier state, and the system must be built so that this does no harm.

afterFigure.text: Both patterns are worth their cost where the read and write needs diverge, or where the history itself is valuable.

lessons.orientation: Tell commands from events, choose between choreography and orchestration, and replay a log of events to rebuild a balance.
lessons.nextAction: Judge which changes to a contract break existing clients, and plan a change without breaking them.

blocks.text: A bank account can be kept as a list of what has happened to it, a deposit here and a withdrawal there, with no balance stored at all, because the balance can be worked out whenever it is wanted by adding up the list from the start. Banks have kept ledgers this way for centuries, and a good deal of software now does the same, by keeping the events that occurred in place of the state that results from them.

Software that keeps events rests on a distinction between two kinds of message: one that asks for something, such as ReserveStock, which the receiver may refuse, and one that records what has already happened, such as OrderPlaced, which cannot be refused.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name a message as a command or an event, say how choreography differs from orchestration, and replay a log to a balance.

recap.keyIdea: Commands ask and may be refused, events record and cannot be, and state can be rebuilt by replaying events at a cost in ordering and duplicates.

blocks.text: A command such as ReserveStock is addressed to one service which may refuse it, and an event such as OrderPlaced is a record in the past tense. Services can be coordinated by reacting to events or by a coordinator, and event sourcing rebuilds state from the log, as 50, 20 and 5 give 35, provided duplicates and ordering are handled.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the contracts between services, and at which changes break a client and which do not.

lead.text: Where two parts of a system meet, one is the **provider** and one the **consumer**, and the **contract** between them is everything the consumer may rely on. It includes the fields and their types, and also what the fields mean, the errors that may be returned and the limits on size and rate. A schema alone is only part of it: a consumer that depends on prices being in pence is relying on something the schema may not say.
A change is **breaking** when a correct existing consumer fails after it. The size of the damage depends on who reads what, which the provider often cannot see.

reveal.text: The provider can tell which fields are read only by asking, or by being told.

lead.text: Adding an optional field to a response or adding a new endpoint leaves everything that clients use untouched, so existing clients carry on. Renaming or removing a field breaks the clients that read it, changing a field's type breaks the clients that parse it, and requiring a new field in requests breaks every client that omits it. Tightening validation belongs with the breaking changes too, because requests that used to be accepted are now rejected.
Adding a field is not always safe. A strict consumer that rejects a message with a field it does not know will fail on the new one, so the safety of an addition depends on how the consumers read.

diagram.alt: Changes sorted by effect on existing clients. Adding an optional response field and adding an endpoint are usually compatible. Renaming, removing, changing a type and requiring a new field in requests are breaking.
diagram.caption: A change is breaking when a correct existing client fails after it.

reveal.text: The change that is safe is the one that adds and does not alter.

lead.text: The program in the earlier question shows the habit. The function calls `get` with a default for `qty`, so a message without `qty` still works, and it never looks at the extra field, so a message with a new field still works. A consumer that reads this way is called a **tolerant reader**.

The habit is cheap and it pays for itself: each addition the provider makes is then safe for this consumer, and a missing optional field is no more than a default. The limit is that it covers only the fields it reads, so a rename of price still breaks it, as it breaks every consumer that depends on price.

reveal.text: The principle is sometimes put as being strict in what you send and liberal in what you accept.

lead.text: A rename is breaking, and it still has to happen sometimes. **Expand and contract** does it in three steps. In the first release the provider *expands*: it sends both `qty` and `quantity`. In the second, clients *migrate* at their own pace, each moving from the old name to the new. In the third the provider *contracts*: once no client reads `qty`, it stops sending it.

At every step each client has a name it can read, so nothing breaks, and the cost is a period in which the provider carries both. A version number does not remove this work. It tells clients that something has changed, but the migration still has to be planned.

afterFigure.text: The provider has to know when the last client has moved. Consumer-driven contracts help, since each consumer publishes the parts of the contract it uses, and the provider can check them before it contracts.

diagram.alt: A field rename in three releases. First the provider sends both qty and quantity. Then clients move to quantity, with some still to move. Finally, when no client reads qty, the provider stops sending it.
diagram.caption: Expand, migrate, contract. Use the buttons to step through the releases.

lead.text: An event is part of a contract, since consumers read its fields, so the rules of this lesson apply to it. The difference is that events are kept. A breaking change to an event therefore cannot simply be contracted away, because the old events remain in the log.
The usual answer is again to be tolerant: new readers handle old shapes, and a new shape is added without altering the meaning of an old one.

reveal.text: A consumer that treats an unknown value as a default would carry on, which is the tolerant habit from the earlier screen.

lessons.orientation: Classify a change to a contract as compatible or breaking, read a message tolerantly, and plan a rename with expand and contract.
lessons.nextAction: Draw an architecture with C4, choosing the level that suits the audience.

blocks.text: A provider that sends the message `{"price": 4, "qty": 2}` has promised more than two field names: that `price` is a number and is in pence, that `qty` is a whole number, and that a request with a bad value will be answered with a particular kind of error. Everything that a client may rely on in this way is the provider's contract with it, and a client written against the message depends on all of it, whether or not it has been written down.
Seen like this, a change to the provider is safe or not according to what its clients rely on, however small the edit is.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which changes break a client, read a message in a way that survives additions, and plan a rename that never leaves a client without a name.

recap.keyIdea: A change is breaking when a correct client fails, and expand and contract lets a breaking change happen in steps that never break one.

blocks.text: A contract covers fields, types, meaning, errors and limits, and the changes that break it are those that remove or alter what a consumer relies on. A tolerant reader makes additions safe, and for a rename, expand and contract adds the new name beside the old, moves the clients and then removes the old one.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to showing an architecture to other people, using the C4 levels.

lessons.title: Showing architecture with C4

reveal.text: The four levels are named on the next screen.

lead.text: Simon Brown created the **C4 model** as a response to box-and-line diagrams that mixed levels and said little. It draws one system at four zoom levels. **System context** shows the system as one box, with the people who use it and the systems it depends on, and it can be shown to anyone. **Containers** opens the system into its separately runnable parts, such as a web app, an API and a database. **Components** opens one container into its inner parts, and **code** shows the classes inside a component, which is rarely drawn by hand since it can be produced from the source.

The figure draws the shop at the first three. Each level adds detail and loses breadth, and each suits a different reader: the context level a product owner, the container level a new developer or an operations engineer, and the component level someone about to change one container.

afterFigure.text: The word *container* here is not a Docker container. A C4 container is any separately runnable unit, including a web app, a mobile app and a database, and the same unit might or might not be run in a Docker container.

diagram.alt: A shop drawn at three levels. Level 1 shows the shop system as one box with a customer, a payment provider and an email service around it. Level 2 opens the system into a web app, an API and a database. Level 3 opens the API into four components.

lead.text: A diagram earns its place by being read without its author present. The first view of the figure has three named boxes and two arrows, and it leaves the reader guessing: is the arrow a request, an event or a copy, and is Service a program, a team or a table?

The second view applies the rules of **diagram hygiene**. Every element has a name, a type and a short description. Every arrow says what it carries, as in "reads and writes (SQL)", and the direction of the arrow follows the direction of the dependency or the data. A key explains the shapes and colours, so that a reader never has to guess what a dashed box means.

lead.text: The four levels show structure, and two supplementary views cover what they leave out. A **dynamic** view shows one scenario as a sequence of calls between elements, such as what happens when a customer pays. A **deployment** view shows where the containers run: on which machines, in which regions, and behind which networks.

Diagrams drift away from the system unless they are maintained, and they are easier to maintain when they are written as text or code, in a form that can be kept in the repository and reviewed in a pull request like any other change.

reveal.text: A component diagram is drawn only for a container whose inner structure someone needs to understand.

lessons.orientation: Choose the C4 level that suits a reader and say what a diagram needs so that it can be read without its author.
lessons.nextAction: Weigh options against quality scenarios, and record a decision in a short decision record.

blocks.text: A diagram of a shop might show the shop as a single box, with its customers on one side and a payment provider on the other, or it might open the shop into a web app, an API and a database, or it might open the API into its controllers and repositories. All three are correct, and each is useful to a different reader, so a diagram that mixes them serves none of its readers well.

Simon Brown's C4 model prevents the mixing by naming four levels of zoom and saying what each one is for, and it adds a few rules that let a diagram be read when its author is not in the room, such as a name, a type and a description for every box and a label on every arrow.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the four C4 levels, choose the one that suits a reader, and say what is missing from a diagram that cannot be read alone.

recap.keyIdea: C4 shows one system at four levels, each for a different reader, and a diagram is readable only if every element and arrow is labelled.

blocks.text: The four levels, context, containers, components and code, each answer a different question, and a container is any separately runnable unit rather than a Docker container. Every box should carry a name, a type and a description, and every arrow should say what it carries, so that the diagram can be read without its author.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson sets out how to weigh options against the qualities that matter, and how to record the decision.

lessons.title: Trade-offs and decision records

reveal.text: The same method gives a number for B on the next screen.

lead.text: A trade-off analysis compares options against the quality attributes that matter, and the usual tool is a **weighted decision matrix**. The figure shows two options and three criteria, with weights 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 that add up to 1.
Option A scores 8, 5 and 6, so its total is 0.5 × 8 + 0.3 × 5 + 0.2 × 6, which is 4 + 1.5 + 1.2, or 6.7.

afterFigure.text: The scores should come from the quality scenarios of the first lesson wherever possible.

lead.text: With these weights B totals 7.5 and A totals 6.7, so B ranks first. The matrix did not decide that. The *weights* did, and a person chose them. The second view of the figure keeps every score and changes the weights to 0.7, 0.2 and 0.1, which makes performance count for far more, and A now totals 7.2 against B's 6.9. The ranking flips.

This is why the matrix is a way of making assumptions visible and not a way of finding the answer. Check the **sensitivity** of the result by changing the weights within a plausible range and seeing whether the winner changes. If it does, the weights are what the team has to argue about, and the argument should be had in the open.

lead.text: Code shows what was decided, and it does not show why. Michael Nygard proposed the **architecture decision record**, or ADR, in a 2011 post as a short document for one decision. It has five fields: a title, a status, the context that forced the decision, the decision itself in a full sentence, and the consequences.

The status is what lets a record be corrected without being lost: a record is *proposed* until it is agreed, *accepted* while it stands, *deprecated* when it is discouraged, and *superseded* when a later record replaces it. The consequences should name what gets harder as well as what gets easier, such as the backups the team must now manage.

afterFigure.text: Records are kept in the repository beside the code, so that a change to the code and a change to the decision are reviewed together.

lead.text: A decision that nothing enforces is slowly worn away. A **fitness function** is an automated check that a chosen property still holds, and it turns a decision into a test. If the decision is that the domain does not import the web framework, as in the lesson on layers and ports, a test can scan the domain modules and fail the build for any that do.

Records are also what a reviewer checks a change against. A proposed change, written by a person or generated by a tool, can be read against the accepted records: does it contradict one, and if so is a new record needed? A change that reverses a decision without saying so is the usual sign of drift, and a record makes it visible.

reveal.text: The same kind of check can enforce a limit on dependencies between modules.
The costs belong in the Consequences section, where a later reader looks for them.

lessons.orientation: Score options with a weighted matrix, test whether the ranking survives a change of weights, and record a decision in a short ADR.
lessons.nextAction: Plan how a running system changes: measure technical debt, compute instability and migrate with a strangler.

blocks.text: In a weighted decision matrix each option is scored against each criterion, every score is multiplied by the weight of its criterion, and an option's total is the sum of those products, so that the total is a weighted average of the scores. The scores describe the options, whereas the weights describe how much the people choosing care about each criterion, and a ranking can reverse when the weights move even though no score has changed.

The weights are therefore the part of a trade-off analysis that deserves the most scrutiny, and the analysis is worth keeping in a form that a reader a year later can use: a short record of the context that forced the choice, the decision itself and what it makes harder, so that the assumptions can be checked when they stop being true.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute a weighted total, see whether the ranking depends on the weights, and write the fields of a decision record.

recap.keyIdea: A weighted matrix makes assumptions visible, and a short decision record keeps the reasons and costs of the choice.

blocks.text: Each option's total is the sum of its scores times the weights, and a ranking that flips when the weights move shows that the weights are the real argument. An ADR records one decision with its context, status and consequences, and a fitness function can enforce it, so the reasons survive and the decision is not quietly reversed.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson looks at changing a running system: measuring debt and instability, and migrating step by step.

lessons.title: Evolving a running system

reveal.text: The next screen gives the measure a name and applies it to other modules.

lead.text: Two counts describe a module's place in the system. Its **incoming** dependencies, written Ca, are the modules that depend on it, and its **outgoing** dependencies, written Ce, are the modules it depends on. Its **instability** is I = Ce ÷ (Ca + Ce), the share of its links that point out. The figure shows three modules. One with four dependents and one dependency has I = 0.2, one with a single dependent and three dependencies has I = 0.75, and one that nothing depends on has I = 1.

A module with few dependents and many dependencies is easy to change, because nothing breaks when it does, so a high I is harmless there. A module with many dependents is costly to change, so it should have a low I and should change rarely. The trouble is a module that is both heavily depended on *and* depending on many others, since it must change often and each change spreads.

diagram.alt: A module with incoming dependencies on its left and outgoing dependencies on its right. With four modules depending on it and one dependency, its instability is 0.2. With one dependent and three dependencies, it is 0.75. With no dependents and two dependencies, it is 1.
diagram.caption: Instability is the share of a module's links that point out. Use the buttons to compare three modules.

lead.text: A **technical debt** is a shortcut taken to deliver sooner, and it accrues interest: every later change that has to work around the shortcut costs more. If the shortcut adds one hour to each change, then after four changes it has cost four hours and after ten it has cost ten.

The metaphor also shows that not all debt is bad. A loan taken knowingly, to meet a date that matters, and repaid soon, is a sound decision, and what harms a project is debt that nobody has noticed or priced. The way to price it is to ask what the shortcut costs per change and how many changes are expected, and to compare that total with the cost of repair.

diagram.alt: Interest on a shortcut. Each later change costs one extra hour. After 4 changes the shortcut has cost 4 hours. After 10 changes it has cost 10 hours, the same as a repair that would cost 10 hours once.
diagram.caption: The cost of a shortcut grows with every change that has to work around it. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: Martin Fowler described the **strangler** pattern in 2004, and named it after the strangler figs that grow around a tree until the tree is gone. A router is placed in front of the old system. A slice of functionality, such as checkout, is built in the new system, and the router is changed to send checkout requests there while everything else still goes to the old system.

The system works at every stage, which is the pattern's strength. Each slice moves when it is ready and can be moved back if it fails, and the old system is retired only when it has no work left. A big-bang rewrite offers none of this, since it delivers nothing until it is complete and then replaces the working system in one step.

diagram.alt: A router in front of an old system and a new one, with four slices of functionality: catalogue, checkout, orders and reports. In four views the slices move across one at a time, until the old system has no work left.
diagram.caption: Slices move from old to new behind the router. Use the buttons to step through.

reveal.text: The router changes only when a slice has been tested in the new system.

lead.text: **Refactoring** means changing the structure of code without changing its behaviour, with tests to show that the behaviour is the same. It is done in small steps, with the tests run after each, and with each feature, instead of as a separate project that is put off until it is too large to start. A shortcut that is repaired a little at a time costs less than a shortcut that is repaired after a year.

Much of the code that most needs it has no tests. In that case the first step is to write a **characterisation test**, which records what the code does *today*, whether or not that is right. The test is not a statement of what the code should do. It is a safety net, and it will fail if a later change alters the behaviour by accident.

reveal.text: Once the structure is better, tests of the intended behaviour can replace it.

lead.text: Few architectures are broken by one decision. They erode through many small changes, each reasonable on its own: a domain module imports a framework to save an hour, a service reads another's table, a shortcut is copied because it was there. Each is a small debt, and together they undo the boundaries that the earlier lessons drew.
A fitness function fails the build when a dependency points the wrong way. A decision record says why a boundary exists, so that a reviewer, human or generated, can see that a change contradicts it.

reveal.text: The client sees the same address before and after the slice moves.

lessons.orientation: Compute instability, price a shortcut as interest, and plan a gradual migration with a router in front.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the whole course: name the decisions, draw the boundaries, and weigh a change before making it.

blocks.text: A shortcut that saves three hours now and adds ten minutes to every later change has cost those three hours back after eighteen changes, and every change after that is paid for at the shortcut's expense. Ward Cunningham compared this to debt in 1992, and the comparison is useful because a debt can be measured and priced: a shortcut can be weighed against the cost of repairing it, and the repair made when it pays for itself.

A system that is already running is changed in the same measured way. Counting which modules depend on which shows where a change is dangerous, and a router placed in front of the old system lets one part at a time be replaced while the rest keeps working.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute a module's instability, work out when a repair pays for itself, and plan a migration that keeps the system running.

recap.keyIdea: A system changes safely when you measure where change is dangerous, price its shortcuts, and replace its parts one slice at a time.

blocks.text: Instability, Ce ÷ (Ca + Ce), shows which modules should change rarely, and technical debt is a shortcut whose interest can be counted against the cost of repair. The strangler pattern replaces a system a slice at a time behind a router, and refactoring under tests, with characterisation tests where none exist, keeps each step safe.

questions.prompt: Every request to a service is now checked against a remote identity service before it is handled, which improves security. Which quality does it cost, measured as the time a request takes?
hints: The check is an extra network call on every request.
The quality is measured in milliseconds.
questions.onCorrect: Latency is the usual name for the delay; the check adds a call to every request, so security is traded against it.

acceptedIdeas: latency
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: latency

misconceptions.feedback: Security is what the check improves. The question asks what it costs.

questions.prompt: A scenario for a search page ends with the clause "in 95% of searches, results appear within 1 second". Which of the six parts is that clause?
hints: Ask which part of the clause a test could count and compare with a result.
One of the six parts is the only one that is always a number.

acceptedIdeas: The response measure, the number a test checks
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The response measure, the number a test checks

questions.onCorrect: The clause gives a share (95%) and a limit (1 second), so a test can count the slow searches and fail the scenario.

choices.label: The stimulus, the event that arrives
The environment, the conditions at the time
The artefact, the part of the system that is hit
The response measure, the number a test checks

misconceptions.feedback: The stimulus is the event that starts the scenario, such as a search arriving. The clause says how many searches must be fast, which is a number.
The environment is the condition the system is in, such as normal load or one server down. The clause gives a share and a time limit, and the environment holds neither.
The artefact names the part that receives the stimulus, such as the search service. The clause says nothing about which part.

questions.prompt: At most how many of 5,000 simultaneous orders may take longer than 2 seconds if 99% must be on time?
hints: The allowance is the share that may be slow.
1% is one hundredth.
Divide 5,000 by 100.
questions.onCorrect: Fifty orders may miss the limit, which is why the scenario gives a test something exact to count.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number that must be on time. The question asks how many may be slow.
5 is one hundredth of 500. Take one hundredth of 5,000.

questions.prompt: Five modules are all linked to one another, with one link for each pair. How many links are there?
hints: Pick one module and count the others it is linked to.
Do that for each module, and notice that every link has now been counted from both ends.
Multiply 5 by the number each module links to, then halve it.
questions.onCorrect: Ten links, and the count follows n × (n − 1) ÷ 2, which grows much faster than n.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of 5 modules pairs with 4 others, which counts every pair twice: 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts each link from both ends. A link between two modules is one link.
That is one link per module. Every module also links to several others.

questions.prompt: A function takes an argument `mode='draft'` and, inside, chooses between two different ways of rendering a page depending on its value. Which kind of coupling does that argument create between the caller and the function?
hints: Ask whether the value is information the function uses or a switch between its inner paths.
The caller can only choose the right value if it knows how the function is built inside.
questions.onCorrect: The caller has to know that the function has two internal paths, which is why a flag couples more tightly than plain data.

acceptedIdeas: A control flag
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A control flag

misconceptions.feedback: The caller reads nothing that belongs to the function, such as a private field. It only passes an argument.
Nothing global is shared here. The argument travels in the call itself, and neither side writes a variable the other reads.
Passed data only has to be understood as a value, such as a number to add. Here the value selects which of two ways of rendering runs, so the caller must know that the function has two inner paths.

choices.label: Shared internals
Passed data
Shared global data
A control flag

questions.prompt: Adding a new tax rule forces edits in five modules, each of which works out tax in its own way. Which smell is this?
hints: One change is scattered across many places.
The name suggests pellets spreading over a wide area.
questions.onCorrect: Shotgun surgery usually means one decision has been written out in several places instead of one.

acceptedIdeas: shotgun surgery
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: shotgun surgery

misconceptions.feedback: Feature envy is a method that uses another class's data more than its own. Here one decision is repeated across modules.

questions.prompt: A method on Report reads six fields of Customer and one of Report itself. Which smell does this show?
hints: The method uses mostly another class's data.
Where should the method live to be near its data?
questions.onCorrect: Feature envy suggests the method belongs on Customer, next to the fields it uses.

acceptedIdeas: feature envy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: feature envy

misconceptions.feedback: That smell is one change spread over many modules. This method simply sits in the wrong class.
A god class does too much. This is one method that prefers another class's data.

questions.prompt: A program is split into five modules by processing step, and each of the five reads lines straight from one shared storage format. The format changes. Which modules have to change?
hints: Ask which modules know the format.
In this split every step reads the storage itself.
questions.onCorrect: All five change, because the format is known to every module and so belongs to none of them.

acceptedIdeas: All five, because each one knows the format
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All five, because each one knows the format

misconceptions.feedback: Every step reads the stored lines itself, so each one contains code that depends on the layout, and not only the first.
Printing is the final step, but the format is read at every step, so the change reaches the earlier modules as well.
The steps stay the same, but each one reads the lines through the format, so each is edited when the format changes.

choices.label: Only the first module, which stores the lines
Only the last module, which prints the lines
All five, because each one knows the format
None of them, because the steps themselves are unchanged

questions.prompt: A caller reads `queue._head.value` to see the next item in a queue without removing it. Why is that a problem?
hints: Ask what the author can no longer change once a caller reads `_head`.
Think about what happens to this caller if the queue is rewritten to use an array.

acceptedIdeas: It depends on an implementation detail that the author may change
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It depends on an implementation detail that the author may change

questions.onCorrect: The name `_head` and the shape behind it are the queue's hidden decision, and a caller that reads them has made that decision shared.

choices.label: It changes what the queue holds, so later pops give other items
It runs slower than a call to `pop`, since it walks the whole queue
It needs an extra import, since `_head` is defined in another module
It depends on an implementation detail that the author may change

misconceptions.feedback: Reading a value changes nothing in the queue. The risk is that the caller now depends on `_head` existing and holding what it holds today.
Speed is not the issue, and a lookup of the head is quick. The issue is the dependency on a detail the author may change.
No import is involved, because the attribute belongs to the queue object. The fault is reaching past the interface.

questions.prompt: Checkout, invoice and report all call `pricing.discount(total)`. The rule inside `pricing` changes from a flat 10% to 10% only above 100, and the signature `discount(total)` stays the same. Which modules have to be edited?
hints: Ask which modules know how the discount is worked out.
The callers see only the signature, and the signature has not changed.
questions.onCorrect: Only `pricing` changes, because it hides the rule and the callers see nothing but `discount(total)`.

acceptedIdeas: Only pricing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only pricing

misconceptions.feedback: The callers use only the signature `discount(total)`, which has not changed, so they cannot see the new rule.
The rule lives in pricing, so pricing is where it is rewritten. The callers just use the number it returns.
Someone has to write the new rule, and it lives in the pricing module, so that module is edited.

choices.label: None, because the callers pick the new rule up by themselves
Only pricing
Pricing and the three modules that call it
Only checkout, invoice and report

questions.prompt: The function `stretch(shape)` first sets the shape's width to 5, then sets its height to 2, and returns its area. `Square` subclasses `Rectangle`, and each setter on `Square` sets both sides. What does `stretch(Square(1))` return?
hints: Follow the two setter calls in order on a Square.
Each Square setter changes width and height together.
The last setter leaves both sides at the same value.
questions.onCorrect: The answer is 4, where a Rectangle gives 10, so Square cannot stand in for Rectangle in code that sets the sides separately.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `set_width(5)` makes both sides 5, then `set_height(2)` makes both sides 2, so the area is 2 × 2 = 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the Rectangle's answer. The Square setters change both sides.
A Square cannot have a width of 5 and a height of 2, so the sides never differ.

questions.prompt: A class has to be edited when billing rules change and also when the layout of a report changes. Which principle does it break?
hints: Count the reasons this class has to change.
The principle named for having one of them.
questions.onCorrect: A class with two reasons to change is edited for each, and each edit risks the other responsibility.

choices.label: Open-closed
Liskov substitution
Single responsibility
Interface segregation

acceptedIdeas: Single responsibility
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Single responsibility

misconceptions.feedback: Open-closed is about adding behaviour without editing. This class has two unrelated reasons to be edited.
Interface segregation concerns what callers are made to depend on, not why a class changes.
Liskov concerns subtypes. Nothing here is a subtype.

questions.prompt: A `Circle` class has a `perimeter` method and no `area` method, and it is put in the same list as `Rect` and `Tri`. What happens when the loop `sum(s.area() for s in shapes)` runs?
hints: Python looks the method up on the object at the moment of the call.
Ask what exists on a `Circle` under the name `area`.

acceptedIdeas: The loop stops with `AttributeError: 'Circle' object has no attribute 'area'`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The loop stops with `AttributeError: 'Circle' object has no attribute 'area'`

questions.onCorrect: Running the loop gives that error. Duck typing needs only the method, and it fails exactly when the method is missing.

choices.label: The loop skips `Circle` and adds up the other shapes
The loop uses `perimeter` instead, since it is the closest method
The loop counts the circle as 0, since a missing method defaults to zero
The loop stops with `AttributeError: 'Circle' object has no attribute 'area'`

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the loop skips an object. Calling a method that is missing is an error.
Python looks the method up by name and does not look for a near match.
A missing method has no default value. The lookup fails and Python raises an error.

questions.prompt: A notifier can send over 3 transports (email, SMS, push) and in 3 formats (text, JSON, XML). If there is one subclass for each combination, how many subclasses are there?
hints: Each transport can be used with every format.
Multiply the two counts.
Three groups of three.
questions.onCorrect: Nine subclasses, and the count is a product, so it grows quickly when either list grows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 3 transports pairs with each of the 3 formats, so 3 × 3 = 9.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two counts. A subclass is needed for each pair, not each item.
That counts the transports only.

questions.prompt: A Sender accepts any object that has a send method, and a test passes in a small fake that records its messages. What is this style of polymorphism, which depends on what an object can do and not on its class, usually called in Python?
hints: The saying is about something that walks and quacks.
It is named after a bird.
questions.onCorrect: Duck typing lets a test substitute a fake, so composition and testing fit together.

acceptedIdeas: duck typing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: duck typing

misconceptions.feedback: Inheritance relates classes. Here the Sender cares only that send exists.

questions.prompt: `Money` is a frozen dataclass with an amount and a currency, and a dataclass compares its fields when two objects are tested for equality. What does `print(Money(5, 'GBP') == Money(5, 'USD'))` show?
hints: A frozen dataclass compares its fields.
Compare 5 with 5 and 'GBP' with 'USD'. Both fields must match for the objects to be equal.
questions.onCorrect: The data differs in one field, so the two Money values are not equal.

acceptedIdeas: False, because the currencies differ
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: False, because the currencies differ

misconceptions.feedback: The amounts match, but the currencies are different, and both fields are compared.
Being the same class is not enough. Equality compares the fields one by one.
That is how an ordinary class behaves, since it compares identity. A dataclass compares fields, so two separate objects with the same data would be equal.

choices.label: True, because both amounts are 5
False, because the currencies differ
False, because two separate objects are never equal
True, because both objects are Money

questions.prompt: Two shipments contain exactly the same parcels for the same address but have different tracking numbers. In domain modelling, are they the same shipment?
hints: Would a customer be content to receive only one of them?
Entities are told apart by something that persists.
questions.onCorrect: An entity keeps its identity as its data changes, which is why a shipment can be re-routed and still be the same shipment.

choices.label: Yes, if they were created on the same day
Yes, because their data is identical
No, because their tracking numbers differ
Yes, if they go to the same customer

acceptedIdeas: No, because their tracking numbers differ
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because their tracking numbers differ

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rule for a value object. A shipment is an entity, so its tracking number matters.
Dates are data. Identity is what makes an entity the same one over time.
A customer could send two identical shipments, and they would still be two shipments.

questions.prompt: In the warehouse a product is a bin location and a weight, and in the catalogue it is a description and a price. What name is given to the boundary inside which a term such as product has one meaning?
hints: The word names a limit.
It is the last of the four terms in the lesson.
questions.onCorrect: Each context keeps its own Product, so a change to the warehouse's does not disturb the catalogue.

acceptedIdeas: bounded context
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: bounded context

misconceptions.feedback: An aggregate groups objects changed through a root. The boundary of meaning has another name.

questions.prompt: A frozen dataclass `Money` is created as `m = Money(5, 'GBP')`, and a caller then runs `m.amount = 6`. What happens?
hints: The dataclass was declared with `frozen=True`.
A value object cannot change: a different amount is a different Money.
questions.onCorrect: A frozen dataclass refuses assignment, so a value object cannot change: a different amount is a different Money.

acceptedIdeas: Python raises FrozenInstanceError, and m still holds 5 pounds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Python raises FrozenInstanceError, and m still holds 5 pounds

misconceptions.feedback: That is how an ordinary object behaves. A frozen dataclass refuses assignment to its fields.
Python does not ignore it. The assignment is refused with an error, so the failure is visible at once.
Assigning to a field never builds a new object. A different amount is a different value, and the caller has to create it, as `Money(6, 'GBP')`.

choices.label: Python raises FrozenInstanceError, and m still holds 5 pounds
m now holds 6 pounds
Python ignores the assignment without a message
Python builds a new `Money(6, 'GBP')` and leaves `m` unchanged

questions.prompt: In sales a customer is a buyer with a credit limit, in shipping it is a name and a delivery address, and in billing it is a payer with a VAT number. What does domain modelling suggest?
hints: Ask how many meanings the word has, and whether one class can serve them all without strain.
Where two contexts meet, they agree only on what passes between them.

acceptedIdeas: A model of the customer in each bounded context, linked by a customer id
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A model of the customer in each bounded context, linked by a customer id

questions.onCorrect: Each context models the customer the way it uses it, and they share only an id, so a change in one does not reach the others.

choices.label: One shared `Customer` class that carries every field and rule of the three
Rename the class to `User`, so that one general word covers all three meanings
A model of the customer in each bounded context, linked by a customer id
Put all three meanings in one table, so the customer's data stays in one place

misconceptions.feedback: One class for three meanings must carry all their fields and rules, and a change made for one meaning risks the other two.
A new name does not change that the meanings differ. The class would still serve three purposes.
The model is not the database schema. One table would not stop the three meanings from pulling the same class in three directions.

questions.prompt: `register(name, repo)` calls `repo.save(name.strip().title())`, and `FakeRepo.save` appends whatever it is given to a list called `saved`. After `r = FakeRepo()` and `register('  ada lovelace ', r)`, which describes the string in the list `r.saved`?
hints: register cleans the name before saving it.
strip removes the spaces at both ends and title capitalises each word.
The fake stores what it is given in a list.
questions.onCorrect: The test needed no database: the fake kept what register passed in, and the list could be checked directly.

acceptedIdeas: The name without its spaces, with each word capitalised
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The name without its spaces, with each word capitalised

misconceptions.feedback: `strip()` removes the spaces at both ends, but `title()` also capitalises each word.
That is the argument as it was passed in. `register` strips and capitalises it before it saves.
`title()` capitalises every word, not only the first.

choices.label: The name without its spaces, with each word capitalised
The name without its spaces, still in lower case
The name exactly as it was passed in, spaces included
The name without its spaces, with only its first letter capitalised

questions.prompt: A test replaces a real key-value store with a small class that keeps its entries in a Python dict, so that a value put in can be read back out. Which kind of test double is it?
hints: It works like the real thing in a small way.
A stub answers with canned values and a mock records calls, so this is the third kind.
questions.onCorrect: A fake can be used in many tests because it behaves consistently, and a stub or mock suits tests that need only one answer.

acceptedIdeas: A fake
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A fake

misconceptions.feedback: A stub only returns canned answers. It has no working implementation behind them.
A mock records the calls it receives so that a test can check them afterwards. It does not behave like the real thing.
A seam is the place where a dependency can be replaced, such as an argument. The replacement placed there is the double.

choices.label: A mock
A stub
A seam
A fake

questions.prompt: A rule allows entry when `age >= 18`. Which pair of test cases pins the rule down at its boundary?
hints: The boundary is where the answer changes.
One case is on each side of the change.
questions.onCorrect: Two cases pin the boundary, and a rule written with `>` in place of `>=` would pass one and fail the other.

acceptedIdeas: 17 and 18
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 17 and 18

misconceptions.feedback: Both are far from the boundary. A rule written as `age > 18` would pass both.
The rule refuses both, and so would `age > 18`, so the pair cannot show where the answer changes.
The rule accepts both, and so would `age >= 17`, so the pair misses a limit set too low.

choices.label: 16 and 17
17 and 18
18 and 19
0 and 100

questions.prompt: A suite has 200 unit tests of 0.01 seconds each, 20 integration tests of 0.5 seconds each and 5 end-to-end tests of 20 seconds each. How many seconds does it take to run in total?
hints: Work out each layer's time separately.
Count times the length of one test.
Add the three layer times.
questions.onCorrect: The five slowest tests take 100 of the 112 seconds, which is why the pyramid keeps them few.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 200 × 0.01 = 2, 20 × 0.5 = 10 and 5 × 20 = 100, so the total is 112 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the end-to-end layer, which is the largest.
That is the unit layer only.

questions.prompt: The domain needs to send receipts, so it defines a `ReceiptSender` interface with one method, `send`, that says in its own words what it needs. In the hexagonal style, what is `ReceiptSender`?
hints: The domain defines it and the outside world plugs into it.
A harbour has them too.
questions.onCorrect: The port belongs to the domain, so whatever actually sends the receipts depends on the domain and not the other way round.

acceptedIdeas: port
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: port

misconceptions.feedback: An adapter is the piece that connects to the real system. The question asks about the interface the domain owns.
An interface is the right kind of thing, but this architecture style gives an interface that the domain owns a more specific name.

questions.prompt: A class `SmtpReceiptSender` implements the domain's `ReceiptSender` interface by talking to a real mail server. In the hexagonal style, what is `SmtpReceiptSender`?
hints: It adapts the mail server to the port's shape.
One of the patterns from an earlier lesson has this name.
questions.onCorrect: The mail adapter imports the domain's port, so the dependency arrow points inward.

acceptedIdeas: adapter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: adapter

misconceptions.feedback: The port is the domain's interface. The piece that connects it to the database has another name.
It does implement the interface the domain owns, and this architecture style gives the piece that connects that interface to the outside system a more specific name.

questions.prompt: A request passes through five services in sequence. Each is 99.9% available, and they fail independently. Roughly how available is the whole chain?
hints: The request needs every one of the five to be up at the same moment.
Multiply the five availabilities together, or compare how long each service is down with how long the chain is.

acceptedIdeas: A little less, about 99.5%
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A little less, about 99.5%

choices.label: More, about 99.99%, since the services back each other up
A little less, about 99.5%
Much less, about 95%
The same as one service, 99.9%

questions.onCorrect: Each service adds a small chance of failure, and five of them multiply to about 0.995.

misconceptions.feedback: Each service can be down at a different moment, and the request fails whenever any one of them is, so the chain cannot match a single service.
The fall is real but small: each service is down only a thousandth of the time, so five of them lose about five thousandths together.
The services here are in sequence, not alternatives, so none of them can stand in for another when it is down.

questions.prompt: A request passes through ten services in sequence, each 99.9% available, and they fail independently. To one decimal place, what is the availability of the chain, in percent?
hints: The chain needs every service in it to be up.
Multiply the availability by itself, once for each service.
The result is a little under the figure for five services.
questions.onCorrect: Ten services give 99.0%, which is about seven hours of downtime in a month.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one service. Every further service in the chain lowers the figure.
That is the figure for five services, and this chain is longer.

questions.prompt: A chain is 99.5% available. In a 30-day month of 720 hours, for how many hours is it unavailable?
hints: Unavailability is what remains after availability.
That is 0.5%.
Take 0.5% of 720 hours.
questions.onCorrect: About three and a half hours a month, from five services that each looked reliable on its own.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time the chain is available. The question asks for the time it is not.
0.5 is the percentage that is unavailable. Apply it to the 720 hours.

questions.prompt: A team ships one deployable unit whose code is divided into modules. The modules may call one another only through interfaces, and the build fails when one reaches past an interface. Which style is this?
hints: Count how many things are deployed.
The style is named for the unit that is deployed and for how its code is divided.

acceptedIdeas: modular monolith
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: modular monolith

questions.onCorrect: One unit with enforced module boundaries is a modular monolith, and any module can later become a service if something measurable demands it.

misconceptions.feedback: Microservices are separately deployable services that communicate over a network. This is one deployable unit.
A tangled monolith lets anything call anything. Here the boundaries are enforced.

questions.prompt: The events are deposit 50, withdraw 20 and deposit 5, but a retry stored the last deposit twice, so the log holds four events. What does a replay give?
hints: The log now holds four events.
The duplicate deposit is applied as well.
Add the second deposit to the usual result.
questions.onCorrect: A duplicated event is applied twice unless each event has an id that the consumer checks.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the duplicate. A replay applies every event it finds.
That counts the duplicate as 10. Each copy of the deposit is 5.

questions.prompt: A provider renames the field price to cost and stops sending price. Three existing clients each read price. What happens to them?
hints: Ask which clients read the field being renamed.
A client keeps working only while the name it looks up still exists.
questions.onCorrect: Every client breaks, because price is the one field they all read.

acceptedIdeas: All three break, because each looks the field up by its old name
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All three break, because each looks the field up by its old name

misconceptions.feedback: A tolerant reader ignores extra fields and defaults missing ones, but price is a field these clients read, so without it they have nothing to work with.
A client that supplies a default does not stop, but it now computes with the wrong value. Either way it has lost the field it reads.
An announcement does not change the clients' code, which still asks for price. They fail on the day the name goes unless they are edited first.

choices.label: None of them break, because tolerant readers ignore fields they do not know
All three break, because each looks the field up by its old name
None of them break, as long as the provider announces the change first
Only the clients that treat a missing field as an error

questions.prompt: A mobile app takes the name and price from each product message, ignores every other field, and shows a stock picture when the image field is missing. Which kind of reader is it?
hints: It tolerates change in the message.
Its name describes how it reads.
questions.onCorrect: A tolerant reader survives the additions that would otherwise break strict clients.

acceptedIdeas: tolerant reader
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: tolerant reader

misconceptions.feedback: A strict reader rejects unknown fields. This one accepts them.

questions.prompt: A diagram shows the shop as a single box. Around it are the customers who use it and the payment provider it calls. Which C4 level is it?
hints: Ask whether the diagram opens the shop up or leaves it as one box.
Look at what surrounds the box: people and other systems.

acceptedIdeas: System context, which shows the system as a single box
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: System context, which shows the system as a single box

questions.onCorrect: The system as one box with its users and the systems it depends on is the system context, the widest level, which anyone can read.

choices.label: Containers, which opens the system into its runnable parts
Components, which opens one container into its inner parts
System context, which shows the system as a single box
Code, which shows the classes inside one component

misconceptions.feedback: A container diagram opens the system up. Here the shop stays one box.
Components sit inside one container, and no container appears in this diagram.
Classes are the narrowest view, and this diagram shows no inner structure at all.

questions.prompt: A diagram of a ticket system shows its mobile app, its booking API and its database as separate boxes joined by labelled arrows. Which C4 level is it?
hints: The parts are the separately runnable units.
The second level.
questions.onCorrect: Level 2 answers what the main building blocks are and how they talk, which suits developers and operations.

acceptedIdeas: containers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: containers

misconceptions.feedback: Components are the parts inside one container, which is the next level down.

questions.prompt: A level 2 diagram is drawn for a system made of a web app, a mobile app, an API, a database and a message broker. Which of these does it show as containers?
hints: A C4 container is not a Docker container.
Each part that is runnable or holds data counts, including a database.
questions.onCorrect: A database is a container in C4, because it is something that has to be running for the system to work.

acceptedIdeas: All five, because each is a separately runnable unit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All five, because each is a separately runnable unit

misconceptions.feedback: A C4 container is any separately runnable unit, and a database has to be running for the system to work, so it is a container too.
A container here is not a Docker container. The same unit may or may not be run in one, and either way it is shown.
The web app, the mobile app, the database and the broker are all parts of the system, and each is separately runnable, so each is a container.

choices.label: Only the web app, the mobile app and the API, because a database is not a program
Only the parts that are run in Docker
Only the API, since the others are outside the system
All five, because each is a separately runnable unit

questions.prompt: A container diagram has a box for the part of the system that takes orders. Which label for the box follows the diagram hygiene rules?
hints: Each element should have a name, a type and a short description.
Check which level of detail a container diagram is meant to show.

acceptedIdeas: Orders API [container: web API]: takes orders and checks stock
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Orders API [container: web API]: takes orders and checks stock

questions.onCorrect: The label gives a name, a type and a short description at the right level, so a reader who never met the author can tell what the box is.

choices.label: Orders API [container: web API]: takes orders and checks stock
Backend: handles everything the customer sees and does on the site
Orders API [container: web API]
Order logic: three controllers, two repositories and a mapper

misconceptions.feedback: It has a name and a description, but no type, and the description is too broad to say what the box does.
It has a name and a type but no description, so a reader cannot tell what the box is responsible for.
That lists components, which belong in a component diagram. A container diagram shows the runnable parts, and the label has no type.

questions.prompt: Weights are performance 0.5, cost 0.3 and simplicity 0.2. Option A scores 8, 5 and 6 on those three criteria. What is A's weighted total?
hints: Multiply each score by its weight.
The three products are 4, 1.5 and 1.2.
Add the three products.
questions.onCorrect: A scores 6.7 out of 10, and the weights decide how much each criterion counts toward it.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the scores without the weights.
That uses the wrong weight on one of the scores. Match each score to its own criterion.

questions.prompt: In March a team records that orders are stored in PostgreSQL. In June a new record moves orders to a document store and names the March record as the one it replaces. Which status does the March record now take?
hints: The statuses are proposed, accepted, deprecated and one more.
The new record takes the place of the old.
questions.onCorrect: The old record is kept, with the status superseded and a link to the new one, so the history stays readable.

acceptedIdeas: superseded
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: superseded

misconceptions.feedback: Deprecated means still in force but discouraged. A replaced decision has another status.

questions.prompt: A fitness function scans 40 domain modules and fails the build for each one that imports the web framework. It finds 3. What happens to the build?
hints: A fitness function turns a decision into a test.
Ask what a test does when even one case breaks the rule.
questions.onCorrect: The decision is enforced by the build itself, so the breach is found when it is made and not a year later.

acceptedIdeas: It fails, because even one breach is enough to stop the build
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It fails, because even one breach is enough to stop the build

misconceptions.feedback: The check fails the build for each module that imports the framework, so a single breach is enough to stop it. The decision is enforced and not averaged.
A warning nobody has to act on is the situation the fitness function exists to avoid. It fails the build so that a breach is found when it is made.
The check has no majority threshold. It fails the build for each module that breaks the decision.

choices.label: It passes with a warning that someone may read later
It passes, because 37 of the 40 modules follow the decision
It fails, because even one breach is enough to stop the build
It fails only if more than half of the modules break the rule

questions.prompt: A module has 1 incoming dependency (Ca) and 4 outgoing (Ce). What is its instability, Ce ÷ (Ca + Ce)?
hints: Ce is the outgoing count and Ca the incoming count.
Add them to get all the links.
Divide Ce by that total.
questions.onCorrect: At 0.8 it is unstable, which is acceptable for a module that few others rely on.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction incoming. Instability counts the outgoing share.
That is Ce alone. Divide it by the total of Ca and Ce.

questions.prompt: A repair would cost 10 hours once. The shortcut it would remove adds 1 hour to each change, and the team makes 4 changes a month. After how many months has the repair paid for itself?
hints: Work out the hours the shortcut costs each month.
That is 4 changes at 1 hour each.
Divide the repair's cost by the monthly cost.
questions.onCorrect: After two and a half months the repair is cheaper than living with the shortcut, which is a measurable reason to do it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The shortcut costs 1 × 4 = 4 hours a month, so the 10-hour repair pays for itself after 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 months.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the repair cost in hours. Divide by the monthly cost of the shortcut.
That is the hours lost each month. Divide the repair cost by it.

questions.prompt: A system has 8 slices of functionality, and 3 of them have been routed to the new system by the strangler approach. What is true of the system at this point?

acceptedIdeas: It works, with 3 slices in the new system and 5 in the old one

misconceptions.feedback: The router sends each slice to wherever it now lives, so the 5 unmoved slices are still served by the old system and the whole keeps working.
The old system is retired only when it has no work left, and 5 slices still depend on it.
The router sends a request for a slice to one system, the one where that slice now lives.

choices.label: Both systems answer every request, and the faster reply is used
It is broken until the remaining 5 slices have moved
The old system can be retired, because the new one is running
It works, with 3 slices in the new system and 5 in the old one

questions.prompt: Before refactoring an untested pricing function, you run it on 50 sample orders and write tests that assert whatever it returns today, including one result that looks wrong. What are these tests called?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: characterisation test

misconceptions.feedback: A unit test checks intended behaviour. This kind records what happens now, whatever it is.

questions.prompt: Checkout and orders have both been moved to the new system, and reports are still in the old one. A request for orders arrives at the router. Where does the router send it?
hints: The router sends each slice to the system where that slice now lives.
Ask where orders lives now.
questions.onCorrect: Orders now lives in the new system, so the router sends its requests there while reports still goes to the old one.

acceptedIdeas: To the new system, because orders has been moved

misconceptions.feedback: The router decides by slice and not by order of arrival. Orders has moved, so the request goes to the new system.
Reports has no bearing on a request for orders. The router decides by the slice that is requested.
A request goes to one system, the one where its slice now lives.

choices.label: To both systems, and it uses the faster reply
To the new system, because orders has been moved
To the old system, because the router always tries the old system first
To the old system, because reports is still there

questions.prompt: A service keeps its customers in a table with a column called `cust`, and only that service reads the table. The column is renamed `customer_id`, and the service's responses to its callers stay exactly the same. What has to change?
