acceptedIdeas: Only the service's own code
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the service's own code

questions.onCorrect: Only the service has the column name written into its code, so the rename is one edit in one place.

choices.label: The service and every program that calls it
Nothing, since a column name is only a label
Only the service's own code

misconceptions.feedback: The callers see only the service's responses, and those have not changed, so they cannot tell that the column was renamed.
The service's queries name the column, so they fail until they are edited.

questions.prompt: Four changes are proposed to a system that other teams build on. Once those teams depend on it, which is the hardest to reverse?
hints: Ask how many other programs have to change when each decision is undone.
Programs outside your code cannot be edited in the same commit.

acceptedIdeas: Changing the file format that nine programs read and write
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changing the file format that nine programs read and write

questions.onCorrect: Nine programs have copied the file format into their own code, so undoing it means asking each of them to change.

choices.label: Changing the file format that nine programs read and write
Renaming a column in a table that only one service reads
Replacing the sorting routine inside one module
Renaming a helper function that two files call

misconceptions.feedback: Only the service that reads the table has the name in its code, so the change stays inside one program.
A routine inside one module is called from that module only, so no other program notices the change.
Two files in one project can be edited together in one commit, so the change reaches nobody outside.

questions.prompt: The measure says 99.9% of requests must succeed. Why does the example take 99.9% away from 100% before it finds the allowance?
hints: What does the test count?
A test can count failures, and 99.9% describes the successes.

acceptedIdeas: The test counts failures, so it needs the share the measure leaves for them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The test counts failures, so it needs the share the measure leaves for them

questions.onCorrect: The measure states what must go right, and a test can only count what goes wrong, so the allowance is the share that is left over.

choices.label: A percentage has to be taken away from 100% before it is used on a count
The measure is written the wrong way round, so it has to be turned over
The test counts failures, so it needs the share the measure leaves for them
One of the two servers is down, so 0.1% of the requests are lost

misconceptions.feedback: A percentage of a count can be taken directly. The subtraction is here because the test needs the share that may fail.
The measure is written correctly: it states the share that must succeed. The example turns it into the share that may fail because that is what a test counts.
The environment says what the system is doing when the requests arrive. It does not remove any requests from the measure.

questions.prompt: A team has three open decisions: the colour scheme of an internal admin screen, the format of the events that six other services will read, and the name of a variable inside one function. They have time to settle only one before coding starts. Which should it be?
hints: Ask which decision other services would start to depend on.
Pick the one that is costly to undo.

acceptedIdeas: The format of the events six other services will read
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The format of the events six other services will read

questions.onCorrect: Six services will copy the event format into their own code, which makes it costly to undo.

choices.label: The colour scheme of the internal admin screen, which many people will see
The name of the variable inside one function, which every reader meets
Whichever decision the team finds easiest to agree on this week
The format of the events six other services will read

misconceptions.feedback: A colour scheme in one screen can be changed in an afternoon without asking anyone, so it can wait.
A local name is visible to one function, so renaming it later costs very little.
Ease of agreement says nothing about the cost of undoing a decision. Care should follow the cost of reversal.

questions.prompt: The author of a `Queue` changes it so that items come out newest first instead of oldest first. Every method name stays the same, yet callers that process jobs in the order they arrived break. Which part of the interface has changed?
hints: Think about which item a caller gets when it takes one out.
An interface covers names, ordering, errors and speed.

acceptedIdeas: The order in which items come out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The order in which items come out

questions.onCorrect: A caller that expects oldest first breaks when the order flips, although no method name has changed.

choices.label: How fast each operation runs in use
The order in which items come out
The errors it reports on a bad call
The names of the operations it offers

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing about speed has changed. What changed is which item comes out first.
No error behaviour has changed. The items are the same, but they come out in a different order.
The names are unchanged, which is why this change catches callers by surprise.

questions.prompt: `Checkout` holds a `Notifier` and calls `notifier.send(message)` when an order is placed. A test has to run `Checkout` without sending any real message. What does the test have to do?
hints: `Checkout` calls `send` on whatever `Notifier` it holds.
Which object can the test supply without editing any existing class?

acceptedIdeas: Hand `Checkout` a small object with a `send` method that records messages
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hand `Checkout` a small object with a `send` method that records messages

questions.onCorrect: `Checkout` depends only on the `Notifier` interface, so the test supplies its own object with a `send` method and no existing class is edited.

choices.label: Edit `Checkout` so that it skips the call to `send` while the test runs
Edit `EmailNotifier` so that it does nothing while the test runs
Hand `Checkout` a small object with a `send` method that records messages
Replace `Checkout` with a copy that never calls `send`

misconceptions.feedback: That changes the code under test, so the test no longer shows how `Checkout` behaves. `Checkout` calls `send` on whatever it holds, and that is the place to substitute.
That changes a real class for the sake of one test. `Checkout` accepts any object with a `send` method, so a test can hand it a different one.
That tests a different class. The test should run the real `Checkout`.

questions.prompt: Three places in the code build a shipping label from the same four fields in the same way, and all three have to change whenever the label format changes. What does the rule of three say to do?
hints: The rule waits for a number of occurrences, and the number is in its name.
Ask whether the three copies change for the same reason.

acceptedIdeas: Write one shared function now, since the third copy has appeared
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Write one shared function now, since the third copy has appeared

questions.onCorrect: By the third copy the shared part is plain to see, so one function can hold it and a format change is made once.

choices.label: Write one shared function now, since the third copy has appeared
Wait for a fourth copy before writing anything shared
Leave all three alone, since repetition is harmless
Leave the copies and add a comment saying they must be kept in step

misconceptions.feedback: The rule names three, not four. The third appearance is the point at which the abstraction is written.
Repetition is tolerated at the second copy and not for ever, because every copy of the same knowledge needs its own edit when it changes.
A comment cannot keep three copies in step. By the third copy the common part is visible, and one function can hold it.

questions.prompt: A base class `Account` has `withdraw(amount)`. A subclass `FixedDeposit` overrides `withdraw` to raise an error, because money cannot be taken out before the term ends. A function that withdraws from every `Account` now crashes on a `FixedDeposit`. Which principle does `FixedDeposit` break?
hints: The subclass cannot be used wherever its base type is.
The principle concerns what a subtype must keep of its base type's promises.

acceptedIdeas: Liskov substitution
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Liskov substitution

questions.onCorrect: A `FixedDeposit` cannot stand in for an `Account`, so code written for `Account`s fails, and it is the hierarchy that has to change.

choices.label: Open-closed
Single responsibility
Liskov substitution
Dependency inversion

misconceptions.feedback: Open-closed is about adding behaviour without editing working code. The crash comes from a subtype that does not keep the promise of its base type.
That principle is about a class having several reasons to change. The fault lies in a subclass that refuses what its base class promised.
That principle is about which side owns an abstraction. The function already depends on `Account`, and the trouble is that one subtype does not behave as an `Account` does.

questions.prompt: A sender uses inheritance, with one subclass for each pair of transport and format, and it has 4 transports and 3 formats. A fourth format, YAML, is added. How many new subclasses does it need?
hints: The new format must work with every transport.
One subclass for each pairing of the new format with a transport.
Count the transports, because the new format needs a subclass for each of them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The new format has to work with each of the 4 transports, so it needs one subclass for each pairing: 4 new subclasses.

questions.onCorrect: Four new subclasses with inheritance, against one new class with composition, which is the gap that widens as the lists grow.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of subclasses that exist already. The question asks how many the new format adds.
That is the total once YAML is added. The question asks only for the new subclasses.
That is what composition needs, one class for the new format. With inheritance the format needs a subclass for each transport.

questions.prompt: A temperature sensor has to tell a display, a logger and an alarm whenever its reading changes, and the sensor should not know which of them exist. Which pattern fits?
hints: The sensor should announce, and others listen.
Which pattern keeps a list of listeners?

acceptedIdeas: Observer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Observer

questions.onCorrect: Observer lets new listeners be added without editing the sensor, which stays unaware of what they do.

choices.label: Observer
Strategy
Adapter
Factory

misconceptions.feedback: A strategy swaps one algorithm behind a call. Here several parts need to react to the same change.
An adapter converts one interface into another, and nothing here needs converting.
A factory decides which class to create, which is not the problem.

questions.prompt: A team builds a plug-in system for report formats, with a registry, a loader and a configuration file. The product has one report format and nobody has asked for another. Which principle from the principles lesson names the mistake?
hints: Nothing varies yet, and nobody has asked for a second format.
One principle says not to build for a need you do not have yet.

acceptedIdeas: YAGNI
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: YAGNI

questions.onCorrect: A plug-in system with one plug-in adds machinery that nothing uses.

choices.label: DRY
Liskov substitution
Single responsibility
YAGNI

misconceptions.feedback: DRY is about the same knowledge being written in more than one place. Here nothing is repeated.
Liskov concerns a subtype that cannot stand in for its base type. There is no subtype here.
Single responsibility is about a class with several reasons to change. The plug-in system is structure built for a need nobody has.

questions.prompt: Your code calls `logger.write(text)`, but the monitoring service your team adopts offers only `send_event(name, payload)`. Which pattern fits?
hints: Your code and the service disagree about an interface.
The pattern is named for fitting one thing to another.

acceptedIdeas: Adapter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Adapter

questions.onCorrect: An adapter lets the monitoring service change without the rest of the program being edited.

choices.label: Singleton
Adapter
Observer
Factory

misconceptions.feedback: A singleton limits a class to one instance, which is a different problem.
Observer notifies many listeners. Here one call needs converting.
A factory chooses which class to create. Here the classes exist.

questions.prompt: A function `is_open()` returns `True` when the time is between 09:00 and 17:00. It reads the clock inside, so a test can see `True` only during opening hours. It is rewritten as `is_open(now)`, with the time passed in as an argument. What does the change give a test?
hints: The clock is a dependency that the function can be given.
Ask who decides the time, before and after the change.

acceptedIdeas: A seam where the test can supply any time, such as 08:59 or 17:00
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A seam where the test can supply any time, such as 08:59 or 17:00

questions.onCorrect: With the time as an argument, a test can pass 08:59 or 17:00 directly, and nothing has to wait for the right hour.

choices.label: A faster function, because the time is no longer looked up
A seam where the test can supply any time, such as 08:59 or 17:00
A record of how many times the clock was read
Nothing, because the function still depends on the time

misconceptions.feedback: The time is still looked up, but by whoever calls the function. What changes is who chooses it.
Nothing is recorded. The function is simply given the time, so the test chooses it.
It still needs a time, but the dependency now comes in from outside, and a test can choose it.

questions.prompt: A rule allows a discount when `10 <= quantity <= 99`. Which set of test cases pins down both ends of the range?
hints: Each end of the range is a boundary of its own.
Each boundary needs one value on each side of it.
questions.onCorrect: Each end of a range is a boundary of its own and needs one value just outside it and one just inside.

misconceptions.feedback: All four are inside the range, so a rule written with `<` in place of `<=` would pass every one of them.
0 and 200 are far outside the range, so a rule that let in 9 or 100 would still pass this set.
None of these is at an end of the range, so a limit set a little too high or too low would pass them.

questions.prompt:

`from dataclasses import dataclass`
`from decimal import Decimal`
`from domain.money import Money`
`import django.http`

Which one breaks the dependency rule?
hints: The rule says source-code dependencies point inward, toward the domain.
Ask which of these modules belongs to something outside the domain.

acceptedIdeas: `import django.http`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `import django.http`

questions.onCorrect: A web framework is an adapter, so the domain importing it points the dependency outward.

choices.label: `import django.http`
`from dataclasses import dataclass`
`from decimal import Decimal`
`from domain.money import Money`

misconceptions.feedback: `dataclasses` is part of Python's standard library. The rule forbids pointing outward to frameworks and databases, and a language library is not one.
`decimal` is also standard library, and the domain can use the language it is written in.
`Money` lives in the domain, so the arrow stays inside it.

questions.prompt: A team adds a method to the domain's `Order` class that returns a web framework's `Response` object, so that the web layer can send it straight back. Which rule does this break?
hints: Source-code dependencies must point in a certain direction.

acceptedIdeas: The dependency rule
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The dependency rule

questions.onCorrect: The domain now cannot be built or tested without the web framework, though it should know nothing of it.

choices.label: The Liskov substitution principle
The rule of three
The dependency rule
YAGNI

misconceptions.feedback: That principle concerns a subtype standing in for its base type. This change makes the domain depend on a framework type.

questions.prompt: An orders service and a stock service are deployed separately, but both read and write the same `stock` table. A developer wants to rename a column in that table. What has to happen?
hints: Ask which services have the column name written into their code.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both teams have to agree, because both services depend on the table

questions.onCorrect: Two services that share a table are not independent, because its layout can change only with the agreement of both.

choices.label: Only the stock team has to act, because the table is named after stock
Nothing beyond the edit, because separate deployment keeps the services independent
Only the team that runs the database server has to act
Both teams have to agree, because both services depend on the table

misconceptions.feedback: Table names do not decide who depends on a table. The orders service reads and writes it too, so a change to it reaches that service.
Deploying separately does not make the services independent while they share a table. Each is tied to the other's use of it.
The people who run the server do not know how each service uses the columns. The two services depend on the table, so the teams that own them have to agree.

questions.prompt: A team reviews the messages that its services send to one another. Which of these messages is an event?
hints: Names in the imperative ask for something.

acceptedIdeas: PaymentTaken
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: PaymentTaken

questions.onCorrect: PaymentTaken is in the past tense because it reports a fact, and a fact cannot be refused.

choices.label: ReserveStock
PaymentTaken
PlaceOrder
CancelShipment

misconceptions.feedback: ReserveStock is in the imperative because it asks the stock service to do something, and the service may refuse. That makes it a command.
PlaceOrder asks for an order to be placed and can be refused, for example when the basket is empty. That makes it a command.
CancelShipment asks for something to be undone and can be refused once the shipment has left. That makes it a command.

questions.prompt: A new order has to reach billing, shipping and analytics today, and other teams add more listeners every few months. Which style suits it, and what does that style cost?
hints: Ask which style is easy to extend with a new listener.
The price of having no coordinator is that nobody holds the whole flow.

acceptedIdeas: Choreography, at the price of a flow that is hard to follow in one place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Choreography, at the price of a flow that is hard to follow in one place

questions.onCorrect: Each new listener only subscribes to the event, but nobody holds the whole flow, so it is harder to follow and to debug.

choices.label: Orchestration, at the price of a flow that is hard to follow in one place
Orchestration, at the price of a central service that every flow depends on
Choreography, at the price of a flow that is hard to follow in one place
Choreography, at the price of a central service that every flow depends on

misconceptions.feedback: Orchestration keeps the flow in one place, so it is the easy one to follow. Its price is the central service that every flow depends on.
Orchestration is built for a few steps that rarely change. Here other teams keep adding listeners, and a coordinator would have to be edited for each.
Choreography has no central service. Its price is that nobody holds the whole flow, so the flow is harder to follow and to debug.

questions.prompt: A provider plans changes to an API that several clients already use. Which change is backwards compatible for those clients?
hints: Which change leaves everything the clients already use in place?
Clients that send nothing new must still be accepted.

acceptedIdeas: Accepting a new optional parameter in requests
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Accepting a new optional parameter in requests

choices.label: Accepting a new optional parameter in requests
Changing the unit of the `price` field from pence to pounds
Lowering the maximum request size from 1 MB to 100 KB
Making an existing optional field required

misconceptions.feedback: The field keeps its name and type, but its meaning has changed, so every client that reads it now gets a wrong value.
Requests that used to be accepted are now rejected, so this tightens validation, which breaks clients.

questions.prompt: A provider is renaming `qty` to `quantity` with expand and contract, and sends both names. Four of its five clients now read `quantity`. The fifth, from another company, has not replied. What should the provider do?

Four clients have moved and one has not.

acceptedIdeas: Keep sending both names until the fifth client has moved
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep sending both names until the fifth client has moved

questions.onCorrect: Until the last client moves, both names stay, and the provider carries the cost of sending both.

Stop sending `qty` after a month, whether or not the fifth client has moved
Keep sending both names until the fifth client has moved
Stop sending `quantity` and go back to `qty`

misconceptions.feedback: The fifth client still reads `qty`, so it breaks the day the name goes.
A deadline does not change what the fifth client reads. The old name can go only when no client reads it.

questions.prompt: A provider adds a new allowed value, `refunded`, to a `status` field that used to be either `paid` or `pending`. Which description of this change is right?

It breaks every client, because every client reads `status`

misconceptions.feedback: A client written for two values may stop on a third, so an addition can still break it.

questions.prompt: In a container diagram, an arrow joins the booking API to its database. Which label for the arrow follows the diagram hygiene rules?
hints: Every arrow should say what it carries.

acceptedIdeas: Reads and writes bookings (SQL)

questions.onCorrect: Naming the data and the protocol tells the reader what crosses the arrow without anyone having to explain.

choices.label: Uses the booking database as storage
Connects to the database for data
Database access layer in the API
Reads and writes bookings (SQL)

misconceptions.feedback: This says the boxes are related but not what the arrow carries, so the reader still has to guess whether it is a request, an event or a copy.
This only says that the boxes are joined, which the arrow already shows.
This names a kind of box and not what travels along the arrow.

questions.prompt: An engineer is about to change how the booking API validates tickets and wants to see the API's inner parts. Which C4 level fits best?

acceptedIdeas: Components

questions.prompt: Option A scores 8, 5 and 6 on performance, cost and simplicity, and option B scores 6, 9 and 9. The weights are now performance 0.6, cost 0.2 and simplicity 0.2. Which option has the higher weighted total?

Option B
They tie

misconceptions.feedback: A's total rises to 7.0 as performance counts for more, but B's total is 7.2, so B is still ahead.

questions.prompt: A team starts a payments product that partner companies will connect to. Once the first release is out, which of these decisions will be cheap to reverse and which will be costly?

items.label: The name of a private helper function inside the checkout module
items.explanation: Only the module's own code calls it, so a rename is one edit.

items.label: Which library the checkout module uses to sort its list of items
items.explanation: The choice sits behind one function, so no caller can see it.

items.label: The field names and units in the JSON that partner companies send and receive
items.explanation: Every partner has written them into its own code, so a change has to be agreed with all of them.

items.explanation: Each reader has the format in its own code, and old events stay in the log.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The button colour, the private function name and the sorting library are cheap to reverse; the partner JSON, the shared table and the event format are costly.

questions.prompt: Four teams each write down what "fast" means for a search page. Which statement is a scenario that a test can fail?
hints: A test needs a load, a share of requests and a time limit.

acceptedIdeas: With 500 users searching at once, 95% of searches return within 1 second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With 500 users searching at once, 95% of searches return within 1 second

questions.onCorrect: It names the load (500 at once), the share (95%) and the limit (1 second), so a test can count the slow searches and report a failure.

choices.label: Search should feel quick to nearly all users, even on busy days
Search should respond in well under a second whenever the site is healthy
Search should be much faster than the old page, as users have asked
With 500 users searching at once, 95% of searches return within 1 second

misconceptions.feedback: "Quick", "nearly all" and "busy" have no numbers, so no test can say the page missed them.
"Well under a second" has no load and no share of searches, so one slow search among a thousand does not show whether it fails.
A comparison with the old page has no limit to test against, and the old page's speed may itself be unknown.

questions.prompt: A login scenario reads: "While one of the two authentication servers is down, 99.9% of 10,000 login requests still succeed." Which of the six parts is the clause "While one of the two authentication servers is down"?
hints: The clause describes the situation the system is in when the event arrives.
Normal operation and a failed server are examples of the same part.

acceptedIdeas: environment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: environment

questions.onCorrect: The failed server is the condition the requests arrive in, which is what the environment part records.

misconceptions.feedback: The stimulus is the event that arrives, which here is the login requests. The failed server is the condition they arrive in.
The response is what the system does, such as serving the request from the other server. The failed server describes the situation before it responds.

questions.prompt: Eight modules each call all seven others directly, which is 28 links. A proposal routes every call through one new hub module instead. Which statement about the proposal is right?
hints: Count the links a single module has before and after, then add them for all eight.
Removing links does not remove the knowledge, so ask who now holds it.

acceptedIdeas: It cuts the links from 28 to 8, and the hub now has to know all eight modules
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It cuts the links from 28 to 8, and the hub now has to know all eight modules

questions.onCorrect: Each of the eight modules keeps one link, to the hub, so 8 links replace 28, and the hub becomes the one module that depends on all of them.

choices.label: It cuts the links from 28 to 8, and the hub now has to know all eight modules
It cuts the links from 28 to 8, so coupling in the system is gone
It raises the links from 28 to 36, since the hub adds eight to the old links
It leaves 28 links, since each module can still reach every other

misconceptions.feedback: Eight links remain, and every one runs to the hub. The hub depends on all eight modules, so the coupling has moved to one place.
The old direct links are removed, because every call now goes through the hub. Only the eight links to the hub remain.
Links count what depends on what, and a module reached through the hub depends only on the hub. Eight links remain.

questions.prompt: Dozens of functions read `order.customer.address.country` directly, and the team expects `Address` to change its layout. Which change does the most to cut the number of places that know that layout?
hints: Ask how many places must change if `Address` renames `country`.
A fix that leaves the chain in every caller has not reduced who knows it.

acceptedIdeas: Add `Order.shipping_country()`, which asks the customer, and have callers use it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Add `Order.shipping_country()`, which asks the customer, and have callers use it

questions.onCorrect: With the method, only `Order` and what it calls know the chain, so a change to `Address` is felt in one place.

choices.label: Copy `country` onto each `Order` as its own field, so callers skip the chain
Keep the chain, and put a comment above each use warning that `Address` may change
Add `Order.shipping_country()`, which asks the customer, and have callers use it
Store the chain in a local variable, `a = order.customer.address`, and use `a.country`

misconceptions.feedback: The copy goes stale when a customer moves, and callers still depend on a field that duplicates the address's layout.
A comment does not stop callers from breaking. Each one still has the layout written into its code.
Each caller still knows that an order has a customer who has an address with a country, so the layout is as widely known as before.

questions.prompt: A code review turns up six problems in one codebase. Which smell is each one?
hints: Ask whether the trouble is one change spread over many places, one method far from its data, or one class doing too much.
Shotgun surgery and feature envy both involve behaviour that sits away from the data or decision it depends on.

items.label: Raising the VAT rate means editing the checkout, invoice, report and email modules
items.explanation: One change to a single rule forces edits across four modules that each work out VAT themselves.

items.label: `Invoice.total_weight()` reads six fields of `Parcel` and none of its own
items.explanation: The method works on another class's data, so it probably belongs on `Parcel`.

items.label: `AppManager` handles login, tax, PDFs, e-mails and discounts, so nearly every pull request touches it
items.explanation: One class holds so many responsibilities that almost every change lands in it.

items.label: A new date format means changing the same formatting line in seven files
items.explanation: The decision about date format is spread over seven places instead of living in one.

items.label: `Report.customer_line()` calls five getters on `Customer` and uses nothing from `Report`
items.explanation: It envies `Customer`, since all the data it uses lives there.

items.label: `OrderService` has 60 methods covering pricing, stock, shipping and refunds
items.explanation: Unrelated jobs sit in one class, so it has a reason to change for each of them.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The VAT edits and the seven-file date format are shotgun surgery, the `Invoice` and `Report` methods are feature envy, and `AppManager` and `OrderService` are god classes.

questions.onCorrect: All three smells come from behaviour that sits far from the data or decision it depends on, and the repair is to move it nearby.

questions.prompt: A module `utils.py` holds `slugify(title)`, `parse_date(text)`, `send_welcome_email(user)` and `retry(fn, times)`. Over a year, almost every pull request edits it. What does that say about the module?
hints: Ask how many different reasons the file has to change.
Cohesion is about what sits inside one module, and coupling is about the links between modules.

acceptedIdeas: It has low cohesion, since its parts share only that they are helpful
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It has low cohesion, since its parts share only that they are helpful

questions.onCorrect: A tax rule, a mail provider and a retry policy have nothing in common, so each lands in the same file and the file is edited for every reason.

choices.label: It has low coupling, since each function is small and stands alone
It is too short, so merging its neighbours in would raise its cohesion
It has high cohesion, since a utility module serves the whole codebase
It has low cohesion, since its parts share only that they are helpful

misconceptions.feedback: Coupling describes links between modules. The pattern here is about what is inside one: many unrelated jobs that each give the file a reason to change.
Merging in more unrelated code adds reasons to change. Cohesion rises when each module serves one purpose.
Serving everyone is not a single purpose. Its functions have as many reasons to change as there are functions.

questions.prompt: A system of 10 modules, all linked in pairs, has 45 links. The team adds 10 more modules and links them the same way. What happens to the number of links?
hints: Use n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 for 20 modules and compare it with 45.
Every new module can link to all the old ones as well as to each other.

acceptedIdeas: It rises to 190, more than four times as many
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises to 190, more than four times as many

questions.onCorrect: 20 × 19 ÷ 2 is 190, about 4.2 times 45, so doubling the modules gives far more than double the routes for a change to spread along.

choices.label: It stays at 45, since links belong to the design and not to the modules
It rises to 190, more than four times as many
It doubles to 90, since the modules have doubled
It rises to 55, one for each new module

misconceptions.feedback: Every new module can link to all the old ones as well as to the other new ones, so the count cannot stay the same.
Links grow with the number of pairs, and pairs grow faster than modules, so doubling the modules more than doubles the links.
A new module links to every module already there, so each one adds many links and not one.

questions.prompt:
A program uses a `Stack` only through `push` and `pop`:

`s = Stack()`
`s.push(1)`
`s.push(2)`
`s.push(3)`
`s.pop()`
`s.pop()`
`print(s.pop())`

The author of `Stack` then stores the items in a linked list instead of a Python list, and `push` and `pop` behave as before. What does the program print, and does it need editing?
hints: Write out the stack after each push and each pop, newest item on top.
Ask what in the program refers to the way the items are stored.

acceptedIdeas: It prints 1 and needs no edit, since it uses only push and pop
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It prints 1 and needs no edit, since it uses only push and pop

questions.onCorrect: The program relies only on the interface, so the author can swap the list for a linked list without asking anyone.

choices.label: It prints 1, but every call has to be edited for the new storage
It prints 3, since the first two pops take the oldest items
It prints 1 and needs no edit, since it uses only push and pop
It prints 2, since the last call to pop is skipped

misconceptions.feedback: The calls name only `push` and `pop`, and those still behave as before. Nothing in the program refers to how the items are held.
A stack gives back the newest item first. The pops remove 3 and then 2, and the third returns 1.
Every call runs. Three pops from a stack holding 1, 2 and 3 leave the third call returning 1.

questions.prompt:
A helper `peek(s)` returns `s._items[-1]`. The author of `Stack` switches the storage to a linked list, and `peek` now stops with this line:

`AttributeError: 'Stack' object has no attribute '_items'`

Which change fixes the cause?
hints: Ask which code should know how the stack stores its items.
A fix that keeps callers reading the stack's internals will fail again at the next change.

acceptedIdeas: Give `Stack` a `peek()` method, and have callers use it instead of `_items`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Give `Stack` a `peek()` method, and have callers use it instead of `_items`

questions.onCorrect: A `peek()` method puts the knowledge of the storage back inside `Stack`, so the author can change it again without breaking any caller.

choices.label: Give `Stack` a `peek()` method, and have callers use it instead of `_items`
Name the linked list's top node `_items` as well, so that old callers work
Make the name public as `items`, so that reading it is allowed
Have callers catch `AttributeError` and fall back to calling `pop`

misconceptions.feedback: That hides the symptom and keeps the leak. The next change to the storage breaks `peek` again.
A public name is a promise to keep it. That turns a hidden detail into part of the interface, which is what the author wanted to avoid.
A `pop` removes the item, so the caller loses the very value it only wanted to look at.

questions.prompt: A function reads `s._items[-1]` instead of calling a method of the stack, so the author can no longer change how the stack stores its items without breaking it. In the lesson's terms, what is this kind of fault called?
hints: The abstraction was meant to hide the storage, and the storage has shown through.
The name uses the word for something that lets something through that it should hold back.

acceptedIdeas: leaky abstraction
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: leaky abstraction

questions.onCorrect: The decision meant to be hidden has been shared with a caller, which is what makes the abstraction leaky.

misconceptions.feedback: Encapsulation is what the stack was meant to provide. The fault is the interface letting a caller reach past it.
Coupling is the general term for the link. The lesson names this particular kind, where a hidden detail has become visible to callers.

questions.prompt:
This helper is used throughout a program:

`def next_job(s):`
 `try:`
  `return s.pop()`
 `except IndexError:`
  `return "empty"`

The author of `Stack` changes `pop` so that an empty stack returns `None` instead of raising `IndexError`. No method name changes. What does `print(next_job(Stack()))` now show?
hints: Follow the call into `pop` on an empty stack, using the new behaviour.
The helper's `except` clause was written for a promise the interface used to make.

acceptedIdeas: None, since the `except` branch no longer runs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: None, since the `except` branch no longer runs

questions.onCorrect: Running the code prints `None`. What `pop` does on an empty stack was part of the interface, so the author broke callers without changing a name.

choices.label: empty, since the method names are unchanged
IndexError, since the stack is still empty
None, since the `except` branch no longer runs

misconceptions.feedback: The `except` branch runs only when `pop` raises `IndexError`, and the new `pop` no longer raises it.
The new `pop` returns `None` and raises nothing, so the helper never sees an exception.

questions.prompt:
These two functions have the same body today:

`def invoice_date(d):`
 `return d.strftime("%d/%m/%Y")`
`def log_date(d):`
 `return d.strftime("%d/%m/%Y")`

`invoice_date` follows the format that tax law requires on invoices, and `log_date` follows what the log-search tool can parse. A teammate wants to merge them into one function in the name of DRY. What should you do?
hints: DRY says each piece of knowledge should live in one place. Ask how many pieces of knowledge these two bodies hold.
Imagine tax law changes the invoice format next year, and ask what happens to the logs if the functions are merged.

acceptedIdeas: Keep both, since each holds different knowledge and may change alone
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep both, since each holds different knowledge and may change alone

questions.onCorrect: The two bodies look alike but answer to a tax rule and a tool, so they have different reasons to change. The rule of three says to wait until the copies share a reason.

choices.label: Keep both, since each holds different knowledge and may change alone
Merge them and add a `kind` flag, so each caller picks its format
Delete `log_date` and have the logs call `invoice_date`
Merge them, since identical code always breaks DRY

misconceptions.feedback: A flag makes every caller know about the function's inner paths, and the two rules still change for different reasons.
A change to the tax format would then reach the logs, so the two uses of one function can break each other.
DRY is about knowledge. Identical text that stands for two different decisions is a coincidence, and merging it ties them together.

questions.prompt: Each new payment method means adding another `elif method == ...` branch inside `pay()`, so code that already works and is tested has to be opened every time. Which SOLID principle does `pay()` strain?
hints: Ask what has to be edited when a new case arrives.
Of the five principles, one says code should be extended without being modified.

acceptedIdeas: open-closed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: open-closed

questions.onCorrect: The principle asks that a new payment method be added without opening `pay()`, for example by passing in a function for each method.

misconceptions.feedback: A function with one `elif` per method may still do one job. The trouble is that extending it means editing it.
Liskov substitution is about subtypes that break what their base type promises, and no subtype appears here.
Dependency inversion is about which way an import points. Here the trouble is that adding a case means editing existing code.

questions.prompt:
This `Checkout` creates its own mailer:

`from smtp_mailer import SmtpMailer`
`class Checkout:`
 `def __init__(self):`
  `self.notifier = SmtpMailer()`

Next month `Checkout` must also notify by push message, and its tests must stop sending real mail. Which design needs the fewest edits then?
hints: Ask who should own the description of what `Checkout` needs from a notifier.
A test can supply a fake only if `Checkout` does not create its own notifier.

acceptedIdeas: Take a `notifier` argument typed to a `Notifier` protocol that `Checkout` defines
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Take a `notifier` argument typed to a `Notifier` protocol that `Checkout` defines

questions.onCorrect: `Checkout` owns the small interface it needs, and any channel or test double that has a `send` method can be passed in, so the arrow now points toward `Checkout`.

choices.label: Add a `PushMailer` subclass of `SmtpMailer`, with `Checkout` still creating the mailer itself
Add an `if channel == "push"` branch inside `Checkout`, so all notifying sits in one class
Copy `Checkout` into a second class that creates a push notifier instead
Take a `notifier` argument typed to a `Notifier` protocol that `Checkout` defines

misconceptions.feedback: `Checkout` would still name a concrete class, so a test cannot swap it, and the subclass inherits mail code that a push message has no use for.
Each new channel is another edit to `Checkout`, and the policy of when to notify stays tied to how each channel works.
Two copies of the same policy must be kept in step, and a test still cannot give either one a fake.

questions.prompt:
A program totals areas with this line:

`total = sum(s.area() for s in shapes)`

`shapes` holds a `Rect` and a `Tri`, each with its own `area` method. A new `Circle` class, also with its own `area` method, is added to the list. What has to change in that line?
hints: Read the line and ask whether it mentions any class by name.
What does the call `s.area()` need from each object?

acceptedIdeas: Nothing, since each shape answers `area()` in its own way
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing, since each shape answers `area()` in its own way

questions.onCorrect: The line names no class, so a new shape with an `area` method joins the sum without any edit to it.

choices.label: It needs an `if` for each class, so that it calls the right formula
Nothing, since each shape answers `area()` in its own way
It must use `isinstance` checks, so that `Circle` is recognised
`Circle` must inherit from `Rect`, so that the loop accepts it

misconceptions.feedback: The call `s.area()` already runs each object's own formula. A test for the kind of object would only repeat what the call does.
The line never asks what class an object is, and a new class needs no recognising. It needs only an `area` method.
The loop accepts any object with an `area` method, whatever its parents. Inheriting from `Rect` would give a circle a width and a height it does not have.

questions.prompt: A `Sender` is built as `Sender(SmsTransport(), XmlFormat())`, so a transport and a format are held as parts. A new `PushTransport` class is written. With which of the existing formats can it be used right away?
hints: Ask what the `Sender` needs from a transport and from a format.
Think about how many classes a new transport costs in each design.

acceptedIdeas: All of them, since the sender holds a format and inherits none
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All of them, since the sender holds a format and inherits none

questions.onCorrect: A new transport is one class, and the pair is chosen when the `Sender` is built, so it works with every format at once.

choices.label: Only `XmlFormat`, the format that the last `Sender` was built with
All of them, since the sender holds a format and inherits none
None, until a new subclass is written for each of the formats
Only the formats that share a parent class with `PushTransport`

misconceptions.feedback: The format is a separate part, chosen when the `Sender` is built, and nothing ties a transport to one format.
That is the inheritance design. In the composed design a new transport is one class that works with every format already written.
Neither part has to share a parent. Each only has to offer the methods the `Sender` calls.

questions.prompt: A team is deciding between inheriting from a class and holding it as a part. Which of these situations call for inheritance, and which for composition?
hints: Ask whether every use of the parent could safely take the child.
If the aim is only to reuse another class's behaviour, ask what holding it would cost.

items.label: A `SavingsAccount` that can stand in anywhere an `Account` is used
items.explanation: Every use of the parent can safely take the child, which is the working test for inheritance.

items.label: A `Circle` that every function taking a `Shape` must accept
items.explanation: Callers treat it as a shape, and it keeps every promise a shape makes.

items.label: A `ReportExporter` that wants to write messages the way `Logger` does
items.explanation: It only wants to use what `Logger` does, so it should hold one and call it.

items.label: A `Stack` that wants the `append` and `pop` of a `list`
items.explanation: Inheriting would hand callers every other list method, such as `reverse`, that breaks the stack's rule.

items.label: A notifier whose transport and format vary independently
items.explanation: Two independent choices in one tree multiply the classes. Held as parts, they only add.

items.label: A `Square` that wants to reuse the code of a mutable `Rectangle`
items.explanation: A mutable square cannot honour what a rectangle's setters promise, so it cannot stand in for one.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The savings account and the circle can substitute for their parents, so they inherit; the exporter, the stack, the notifier and the square only want to use what another class does, so they hold it.

questions.onCorrect: Inherit when the child can safely stand in for the parent, and compose when you only want to use what another class does.

questions.prompt:
A developer writes `Stack` by inheriting from `list`, to reuse `append` and `pop`. A caller then reverses it in place:

`class Stack(list):`
 `def push(self, x):`
  `self.append(x)`
`s = Stack()`
`s.push(1)`
`s.push(2)`
`s.push(3)`
`s.reverse()`
`print(s.pop())`

hints: Count how many list methods could break the stack's rule.
Ask which design would let callers use only the operations the stack promises.

acceptedIdeas: Hold a list inside `Stack` and offer only `push` and `pop`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hold a list inside `Stack` and offer only `push` and `pop`

questions.onCorrect: Running the code prints 1. Holding the list as a part exposes only `push` and `pop`, so no caller can reach the methods that break the rule.

choices.label: Override `reverse` so that it raises an error, since that call caused the fault
Write in the class docstring that callers must not call `reverse`
Add a second subclass that also forbids `insert` and `sort`
Hold a list inside `Stack` and offer only `push` and `pop`

misconceptions.feedback: `insert`, `sort`, `remove` and others break the rule in the same way. Patching them one at a time never ends.
A note does not stop the call. The class still hands every list method to every caller.
Each subclass forbids a few more methods and still inherits the rest. The base class stays wider than the stack's promise.

questions.prompt: A notifier has three independent choices, each with 4 options: transport, format and compression. With inheritance there is one subclass for each combination, and with composition each option is one class held by the `Sender`. How do the class counts compare?
hints: Inheritance multiplies the number of options in each choice, and composition adds them.
Use three factors of 4 for one count and three terms of 4 for the other.

acceptedIdeas: 64 subclasses against 12 parts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 64 subclasses against 12 parts

questions.onCorrect: 4 × 4 × 4 is 64 combinations, while 4 + 4 + 4 is 12 parts, and each new option adds one class in the composed design and a whole layer in the inherited one.

choices.label: 64 subclasses against 12 parts
16 subclasses against 12 parts
12 subclasses against 12 parts, since each choice has 4 options
81 subclasses against 12 parts

misconceptions.feedback: 16 counts the combinations of two choices. There are three choices, so there are 4 × 4 × 4 combinations.
Adding the options gives the parts for composition. Inheritance needs a subclass for every combination, which is a product.
81 is 3 to the power 4, with the numbers swapped. Three choices of 4 options give 4 × 4 × 4.

questions.prompt:

`class Subject:`

`log = []`

questions.prompt:

questions.prompt: A team meets six problems in one project. Which pattern answers each one?
hints: Name the problem first: many parts reacting to one change, an algorithm to swap, two interfaces that do not match, or where to create objects.
Each pattern is the answer to one of those problems.

items.label: Several screens must refresh when a price changes, and the price source should not know which screens exist
items.explanation: The source announces the change and each screen subscribes, so the source depends on none of them.

items.label: An audit log and an alarm must both hear about every failed login
items.explanation: Two listeners react to one event, and a third can be attached without editing the login code.

items.label: A report sorts its rows by name, date or amount, as the user chooses
items.explanation: The sorting rule is passed in, so the report code stays the same for every choice.

items.label: A pricing function takes the discount rule as an argument, so the rule can be swapped
items.explanation: The varying algorithm is an argument, which is the pattern in Python.

items.label: Your code calls `mailer.send(to, body)`, but the new provider's library offers `deliver(message)`
items.explanation: The two interfaces do not match, so a small class translates one into the other.

items.label: Callers ask for a notifier by kind, such as "sms", and must not name the classes
items.explanation: One function decides which class to create, so callers never depend on the concrete ones.
