questions.onCorrect: Each pattern is named after the problem it answers, so recognising the problem is the skill and the name follows from it.

questions.prompt: A team writes `IUserStore`, `UserStoreImpl` and `UserStoreFactory` for the one place the app reads users. There is one implementation, one caller, and nobody has asked for a second store. What should the team do?
hints: Ask what varies here, and how many things use the store.
The usual advice is to write the plain code first and introduce the pattern when the problem is real.

acceptedIdeas: Write one plain `UserStore` class, and add an interface when a second store arrives
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Write one plain `UserStore` class, and add an interface when a second store arrives

questions.onCorrect: With nothing varying, the extra classes add indirection and no benefit, and a second store, if it ever comes, shows what the interface should hold.

choices.label: Keep all three, since an interface in front of every class is good practice
Keep the interface and factory, so that adding a second store later is cheap
Write one plain `UserStore` class, and add an interface when a second store arrives
Replace the three with a singleton, since there is only one store

misconceptions.feedback: An interface with one implementation and one caller solves no problem, and every reader must follow an extra step to find the code that runs.
The guess about a later need is often wrong, and the unused structure must still be read and maintained until then. YAGNI says to wait.
A singleton is another pattern applied with no problem to solve. A plain class is all that is needed.

questions.prompt:
An `Order` keeps its lines and a stored total. Code edits a line directly instead of asking the order:

`class Order:`
 `def __init__(self):`
  `self.lines = []`
  `self.total = 0`
 `def add_line(self, price, qty):`
  `self.lines.append({"price": price, "qty": qty})`
  `self.total += price * qty`
`order = Order()`
`order.add_line(500, 2)`
`order.add_line(300, 1)`
`order.lines[1]["price"] = 350`
`print(order.total, sum(l["price"] * l["qty"] for l in order.lines))`

It prints `1300 1350`. What does the output show?
hints: Work out the total that the lines now add up to, and compare it with the stored one.
Only one method updates the stored total. Ask whether the edit went through it.

acceptedIdeas: The stored total no longer equals the lines, since the edit skipped `add_line`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The stored total no longer equals the lines, since the edit skipped `add_line`

questions.onCorrect: The invariant that the total equals the sum of the lines was broken by code that never meant to break it, which is why an aggregate lets only its root change the lines.

choices.label: The stored total no longer equals the lines, since the edit skipped `add_line`
Both figures are right, since 1300 was correct when it was stored
The lines are wrong, since the stored total is the figure the order protects
Python recalculates the total on read, so the gap is only a display delay

misconceptions.feedback: The stored total was right for the old line. The line changed, so the two figures now describe different orders.
The edit made the line what the caller wanted. The fault is that nothing updated the total to match.
The total is a stored number that `add_line` updates, and nothing recalculates it. The gap stays.

questions.prompt: The business rule says an order may have at most 10 lines. The team wants the rule to hold whatever code touches an order. Where should it be enforced?
hints: An invariant needs one place that every change must pass through.
Ask which object can see all the lines at once.

acceptedIdeas: In `Order.add_line`, the only way in to the lines
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In `Order.add_line`, the only way in to the lines

questions.onCorrect: The root sees every line and is the only way to add one, so a rule checked there cannot be bypassed.

choices.label: In the screen with the Add button, which stops offering it at 10 lines
In `OrderLine`, which refuses to be created when the order is full
In `Order.add_line`, the only way in to the lines
In a nightly report that lists the orders with more than 10 lines

misconceptions.feedback: Other code, such as an import job or a second screen, can still add lines. The rule must live where every addition passes.
A line knows nothing about the other lines on its order, so it cannot count them.
A report finds a broken rule after the fact, and the rule would not hold in between.

questions.prompt: A shop models its domain. Which of these are entities, to be told apart by an identity, and which are value objects, where any equal one will do?
hints: Ask whether you would care which one you have, or whether any equal one will do.
An entity can change its data and remain the same thing.

items.label: A customer account that gains orders and a new address over the years
items.explanation: It stays the same account as its data changes, so it needs an id.

items.label: Five pounds sterling as an amount and a currency
items.explanation: Any five pounds is as good as any other, so equal data means equal values.

items.label: A shipment with tracking number 7731, whatever parcels it holds
items.explanation: Two shipments with the same contents are still two shipments, and the tracking number tells them apart.

items.label: A date range from 1 March to 7 March
items.explanation: It is defined entirely by its two dates and does not change.

items.label: The delivery address written on a parcel label
items.explanation: Only what the address says matters, and not which copy of it you hold.

items.label: An order that is placed, paid and shipped and stays the same order
items.explanation: Its data changes through its life, and the order id is what persists.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The account, the shipment and the order are entities; the five pounds, the date range and the label address are value objects.

questions.onCorrect: If you would care which one you have, it is an entity and needs an id, and if any equal one will do, it is a value.

questions.prompt: A domain expert says a refund belongs to one line of an order, because a customer may return one item and keep the rest. The code has `Refund(order_id, amount)`, and its tests only refund whole orders. What does the mismatch suggest?
hints: Ask whose vocabulary the code should use.
If the code cannot say which line, it cannot protect any rule about lines.

acceptedIdeas: The model should follow the expert, so that a refund refers to an order line
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The model should follow the expert, so that a refund refers to an order line

questions.onCorrect: A ubiquitous language means the code uses the expert's words and structure, so a refund that belongs to a line is modelled as one.

choices.label: The model should follow the expert, so that a refund refers to an order line
The expert should be told that refunds are per order, since the code is what runs
Nothing, since an order id is enough to find the lines later
A `reason` field should be added, so that partial refunds can be described in text

misconceptions.feedback: The code is meant to model the business, so the business is the source of truth. A refund per order cannot express a returned item.
Finding the lines later does not say which line was refunded. The mismatch hides the very fact the expert named.
Text cannot be checked by the rules, such as refunding no more than the line cost. The structure itself has to carry it.

questions.prompt: A legacy function `close_shop()` reads the clock, saves to a database and sends a mail, and it has no tests. The team wants to test it on 29 February without changing what it does today. In what order do they work?
hints: The behaviour has to be recorded before the code is changed, or nothing shows whether the change was safe.
A new test only makes sense once the seam exists, and the seam is only trusted once the old behaviour has been checked.

items: Run the function on a few real inputs and record what it returns and does
Add a `now` parameter that defaults to the real clock, so existing calls are unchanged
Check that the recorded behaviour still holds for the existing calls
Write a test that passes 29 February as `now`
Give the database and the mailer the same kind of seam and fake them

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Record the behaviour first. Add the `now` seam with a default so existing calls are unchanged, and check the record still holds, before writing the 29 February test and adding seams for the database and the mailer.

questions.onCorrect: The record comes first so that the first change can be checked against it, and each seam is added in a way that leaves existing callers working.

questions.prompt: A test replaces the mailer with a mock and checks that `send` was called once with `("ada", "Welcome")`. A refactor makes the code call `send_many([("ada", "Welcome")])` instead. Ada still receives the same mail, yet the test fails. What does this show?
hints: Ask what the user can observe, and what the test is actually checking.
A test that replaces everything with mocks ends up testing the mocks.

acceptedIdeas: It checks the calls the code makes, so a fake that records sent mail serves better
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It checks the calls the code makes, so a fake that records sent mail serves better

questions.onCorrect: A fake that records the mail sent lets the test check the result, so a refactor that keeps the result leaves the test passing.

choices.label: The refactor changed the behaviour, since a different method is now called on the mailer
Mocks fail whenever code changes, so a test should never replace the mailer with a double
The test needs a second assertion that counts the calls to `send_many` as well
It checks the calls the code makes, so a fake that records sent mail serves better

misconceptions.feedback: Ada gets the same mail, so the behaviour a caller cares about is unchanged. Only the internal call is different.
A test should replace the mailer, because it must not send real mail. The question is which double: one that records outcomes serves better than one that insists on calls.
More assertions on calls tie the test even closer to how the code works, and the next refactor will break it again.

questions.prompt: A system has four layers: presentation, application, domain and data. In a strict design each layer may call only the layer directly below it. A developer makes a screen in the presentation layer query the data layer directly, to save a call. Which statement is right?
hints: Count the layers between presentation and data.
Ask whether a strict design lets a layer skip the one below it.

acceptedIdeas: It breaks strict layering, since presentation may call only the layer below
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It breaks strict layering, since presentation may call only the layer below

questions.onCorrect: Strict layering allows three arrows for four layers, and a call that skips one is a fourth, which is the shortcut relaxed layering permits.

choices.label: It is allowed, since a layer may call any layer that lies below it
It breaks strict layering, since presentation may call only the layer below
It is allowed in both designs, since the data layer sits at the very bottom
It breaks the design, since no layer may ever call the data layer

misconceptions.feedback: That describes relaxed layering. In a strict design a layer calls only the one directly beneath it.
Position at the bottom does not make a layer open to everyone. A strict design gives the data layer only one caller.
The data layer is called by the layer above it. What is wrong is the screen reaching past two layers to get there.

questions.prompt: A relaxed design lets presentation code read tables in the data layer directly. The data layer renames the column `cust_nm` to `customer_name`. What does the shortcut cost?
hints: Ask which code has the column name written into it.
Each extra arrow is a place where a change can spread.

acceptedIdeas: Screens that read the column break too, so a storage change reaches the top
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Screens that read the column break too, so a storage change reaches the top

questions.onCorrect: Each caller that skips a layer gains one more dependency on the layer it skipped to reach, so a change at the bottom can show up at the top.

choices.label: Nothing, since presentation and data are far apart in the diagram
Screens that read the column break too, so a storage change reaches the top
Only the application layer has to change, since it sits between the other two
The rename is refused, since layering rules do not allow it

misconceptions.feedback: Distance in the diagram does not stop a dependency. A screen that reads `cust_nm` fails when the column changes.
The application layer is skipped by this shortcut, so it cannot protect the screens that read the table themselves.
A layering rule does not stop a rename. It only decides who is allowed to depend on the name.

questions.prompt: A function `total_with_tax(price, rate_port)` returns `price + price * rate_port()`, where `rate_port` is any function that returns the tax rate. Running `total_with_tax(100, lambda: 0.2)` gives `120.0`. In production the rate comes from a database. What does the test show about the design?
hints: Ask what the test had to set up before it could call the function.
Think about how many different things could be passed as `rate_port`.

acceptedIdeas: The function never learns where the rate comes from, so a test needs no database
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The function never learns where the rate comes from, so a test needs no database

questions.onCorrect: The function sees only a callable, so a database adapter in production and a lambda in a test are interchangeable.

choices.label: The function is untestable until the database is replaced by a real tax service
The function depends on the database, since it calls `rate_port` to get the rate
The result 120.0 proves that the production rate is 0.2
The function never learns where the rate comes from, so a test needs no database

misconceptions.feedback: The port is what makes it testable. A lambda stands in for the database without any real service.
It depends on whatever is passed in, and the test passes a lambda. The database is one adapter among those that could be passed.
The test supplied 0.2 itself. It shows that the function applies whatever rate it is given, and says nothing about the production rate.

questions.prompt: A team divides a shop into presentation, application, domain and data layers. Which layer does each of these responsibilities belong to?
hints: Ask which layer would change if the web page were replaced by a command line, and which would not.
Rules of the business hold whatever the screen or the database does.

items.label: Showing a price as £12.50 on a web page
items.explanation: How a value looks to a person is the job of the layer that talks to people.

items.label: Rejecting a form whose email field is empty
items.explanation: It checks what the user typed before anything reaches the rules of the business.

items.label: Placing an order: load the basket, apply the rules, save it and send the receipt
items.explanation: It coordinates a use case and makes the other layers do the work.

items.label: A refund may not exceed the amount paid
items.explanation: It is a rule of the business that holds whichever screen or database is used.

items.label: Free delivery applies to orders of 50 or more
items.explanation: It is a business decision, with no interest in how the page or the table looks.

items.label: Writing the order to the `orders` table
items.explanation: Storage details such as table and column names belong in the layer that knows them.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Formatting the price and rejecting the empty field are presentation, placing the order is application, the refund limit and free delivery are domain, and writing to the table is data.

questions.onCorrect: Each responsibility sits in the layer that changes for the same reason it does, so a new screen or a new database leaves the domain rules alone.

questions.prompt: The column `cust_nm` is copied as `order.cust_nm`, then as `dto.cust_nm`, then as a field of the JSON that clients read. Renaming the column reaches every layer. Which change keeps the next rename inside one layer?
hints: Ask which layer should own the knowledge of column names.
The domain should define what it needs and the database code should satisfy it.

acceptedIdeas: Put an `OrderRepository` port in the domain, so that only the adapter knows column names
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Put an `OrderRepository` port in the domain, so that only the adapter knows column names

questions.onCorrect: The adapter alone knows the column names, so a rename is one edit there and the domain and clients see the same fields as before.

choices.label: Put an `OrderRepository` port in the domain, so that only the adapter knows column names
Move the name into one shared constant, so that every layer imports it from there
Let the presentation layer read the table itself, so that there are fewer copies of it
Rename the field to `cust_nm` in every layer too, so that the names always match up

misconceptions.feedback: Every layer would still import the storage name, so a rename still reaches them and now they all depend on a shared module.
That adds a dependency from the top layer to storage and puts the column name in more places.
Matching names tie every layer to the storage name, which is the trouble to begin with.

questions.prompt: A 150-line script reads one CSV file and writes one row to a database. It runs from the command line only and has one rule, checked in a single function. A colleague proposes a domain package, ports and adapters. What do you advise?
hints: Ask what varies here: the inputs, the rules or the storage.
The structure pays where rules are rich or inputs vary.

acceptedIdeas: Keep it plain, since the structure would be more work than the program
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep it plain, since the structure would be more work than the program

questions.onCorrect: Ports and adapters pay off when the rules are rich or the inputs vary, and neither is true of this script.

choices.label: Add the ports now, since every program should start with the full structure
Add only the ports for the CSV and the database, so that tests need no files
Keep it plain, since the structure would be more work than the program
Rewrite it as three services, so each part can scale alone

misconceptions.feedback: Each port is another interface and each adapter another file. For a script with one input and one rule they add work and no benefit.
A small script can be tested by calling its one function with values. The ports would cost more than the tests save.
Nothing in the description needs scaling, and three services would add network failures to a 150-line script.

questions.prompt: A company wants a checkout service, a catalogue service and a stock service with clean interfaces between them. All 12 of its developers sit in one team and talk about everything all day. Conway's law says that a design copies the communication of the people who build it. What should the company do first?
hints: Conway's law says a design copies the communication structure of the organisation that builds it.
If the structure of the teams is the cause, ask which one you would change to get the design you want.

acceptedIdeas: Form three teams that each own one service, so that talk matches the interfaces wanted
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Form three teams that each own one service, so that talk matches the interfaces wanted

questions.onCorrect: Three teams that each own a service put the communication paths where the interfaces should be, so the design is pulled toward them and not away.

choices.label: Draw the three interfaces in a design document and ask the team to respect them
Keep one team, and add a rule that the services may not share a database
Build one unit and rename its folders as services, so the boundaries look clean
Form three teams that each own one service, so that talk matches the interfaces wanted

misconceptions.feedback: A document does not change who talks to whom. The design will follow the team's communication, which has no seams.
The rule helps, but the team's habit of talking about everything still pulls the services together over time.
Names do not make boundaries. Changes will still pass through every folder, because the people who make them do.

questions.prompt: A team runs a modular monolith. Which of these is a measurable reason to split one module out into its own service?
hints: A measurable reason is one that you could show with numbers, such as load or a blocked team.
Ask what a service gives that a module boundary inside one unit does not.

acceptedIdeas: It needs twenty times the servers of the rest, and scaling the whole unit for it is costly
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It needs twenty times the servers of the rest, and scaling the whole unit for it is costly

questions.onCorrect: A part that needs to scale alone is the kind of demand that a service meets, and the cost of the split can be set against a number.

choices.label: The module has grown past 5,000 lines, and a service would keep each of its files short
It needs twenty times the servers of the rest, and scaling the whole unit for it is costly
Two developers would like to write the module in a different language of their own choice
Services are the modern style, and the team does not want to be left behind by it

misconceptions.feedback: Length is not a need that a network call can meet. A long module can be split into smaller modules inside the same unit.
A preference is not something that the system measures. It would add network calls and a second set of tools for a taste.
A style is not a reason. Services add network failures, data spread across services and more to run, which must be paid for by a gain.

questions.prompt: A team of six starts a new product whose parts are not yet clear. One engineer proposes ten microservices from the first day. What do you advise?
hints: Ask how well the team knows where the boundaries belong.
Compare what it costs to move a wrong boundary inside one unit and between services.

acceptedIdeas: Start with a modular monolith, and split a module when something measurable demands it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Start with a modular monolith, and split a module when something measurable demands it

questions.onCorrect: Boundaries can be moved cheaply while they are still wrong, so a team of six learns where they belong before paying for the network.

choices.label: Agree, since services are cheaper to change than modules once they exist
Agree, but let the ten services share one database so that they stay consistent
Start with a modular monolith, and split a module when something measurable demands it
Start with a tangled monolith, since boundaries take time that the product does not have

misconceptions.feedback: Every call between services can fail or be slow, and moving a boundary between services is far more work than moving one between modules.
Services that share a table are not independent, because the table's schema can change only with every team's agreement.
A tangled unit lets every change spread. Modules with enforced boundaries cost little and keep the options open.

questions.prompt: A request needs five services in sequence, each 99.95% available, and they fail independently. A teammate says that each service is above 99.9%, so the chain must be above 99.9% too. Is the teammate right?
hints: For a chain in which every service is needed, multiply the availabilities.
Work out 0.9995 to the power 5 and compare it with 0.999.

acceptedIdeas: No, the chain is about 99.75%, since availabilities multiply along it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, the chain is about 99.75%, since availabilities multiply along it

questions.onCorrect: 0.9995 multiplied by itself five times is about 0.9975, below 0.999, so a chain of reliable parts can fall short of the limit that each of them meets.

choices.label: No, the chain is about 99.75%, since availabilities multiply along it
Yes, since a chain is only as weak as its weakest service
No, the chain is about 99.5%, since each service adds 0.1% of downtime
Yes, since the services back each other up when one is down

misconceptions.feedback: A chain fails when any one service fails, so the failures add up. Being as good as the weakest link would need the services to fail together.
Each service is down 0.05% of the time, since 100% − 99.95% = 0.05%, and the five of them add up to about 0.25%.
In a chain every service is needed for each request, so none backs another up. Redundancy would need services in parallel.

questions.prompt: An account stores only its current balance, which is 35. An auditor asks what the balance was last Tuesday and how it came to be 35. What can the system answer?
hints: Ask what the system holds after a change has been applied.
Compare it with a ledger, which keeps every entry.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing about the past, since each change overwrote the number before it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing about the past, since each change overwrote the number before it

questions.onCorrect: Storing the state loses how it came to be, which is the gap that storing the events instead fills.

choices.label: Everything, since a balance of 35 can be reached in only one way
Only the changes since Tuesday, which can be subtracted from 35
Nothing about the past, since each change overwrote the number before it
The whole history, since databases always keep the old values

misconceptions.feedback: Many different histories end at 35. The number alone does not say which one happened.
The system holds no list of changes to subtract. It holds only the latest number.
A database keeps old values only if it was built to. Updating a stored number replaces it.

questions.prompt: In an event-sourced account, a clerk enters `withdraw 45` when the customer took out 40. The log holds deposit 100, withdraw 30 and withdraw 45, so a replay gives 25 and the right figure is 30. How should the mistake be corrected?
hints: In a ledger, a wrong entry is corrected by another entry.
Ask which approach keeps both the history and the right balance.

acceptedIdeas: Append a correcting event, such as deposit 5, and keep the wrong one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Append a correcting event, such as deposit 5, and keep the wrong one

questions.onCorrect: Replaying all four events gives 100 − 30 − 45 + 5 = 30, and the log still shows what happened, including the correction.

choices.label: Append a correcting event, such as deposit 5, and keep the wrong one
Edit the third event so that it reads `withdraw 40`
Delete the third event and enter `withdraw 40` as a new one
Overwrite the stored balance with 30, since the state is what is read

misconceptions.feedback: Rewriting an event hides what was recorded, and consumers that already read it keep the wrong figure.
A deleted event leaves no trace that a mistake was made, and consumers that applied it never learn of the change.
A stored balance beside the log can disagree with a replay, and the next rebuild brings the 25 back.

questions.prompt: A refund flow uses choreography. Payments listens for `RefundRequested`, Accounting listens for `RefundIssued`, and Email listens for `LedgerAdjusted`. In what order do these steps happen?
hints: Each service starts only when the event it listens for has been announced.
Follow the events from the one nobody listens to first, to the one that ends the chain.

items: Support announces `RefundRequested`
Payments returns the money and announces `RefundIssued`
Accounting adjusts the ledger and announces `LedgerAdjusted`
Email tells the customer that the refund is done

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Support announces RefundRequested, Payments returns the money and announces RefundIssued, Accounting adjusts the ledger and announces LedgerAdjusted, and Email tells the customer, because each service reacts to the event before it.

questions.onCorrect: Each service reacts to the previous event, so nobody holds the whole flow and it shows only in the events as they pass.

questions.prompt: A customer changes their address. The profile page, which is served from a read model built from events, shows the old address for about a second. Is this a bug?
hints: Ask how the read model learns of a change made to the write model.
A reader may briefly see the earlier state, and the system has to be built so that this does no harm.

acceptedIdeas: Not necessarily, since the read model updates from events and may briefly lag
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not necessarily, since the read model updates from events and may briefly lag

questions.onCorrect: A read model fed by events is eventually consistent, so a short lag is a property of the design, and the screens must be built to cope with it.

choices.label: Yes, since the read model should be updated in the same step as the write
Yes, since a read model loses events and so cannot show what was saved
No, since a delay of a second is always harmless
Not necessarily, since the read model updates from events and may briefly lag

misconceptions.feedback: Updating it in the same step would tie the two models together. The design accepts a brief lag instead.
The read model updates from the events, and none is lost. It is a moment behind and then catches up.
Whether a delay is harmless depends on what the screen is used for. The design must make sure that the lag does no harm.

questions.prompt: A team publishes a message named `UpdateInventory` to every service, to announce that stock levels have changed. The name reads like a command, though the message reports a fact. In which tense should an event like this be named?
hints: Ask whether the message asks for something or reports something that is already true.
A command names what it asks for, and an event names what has happened.

acceptedIdeas: past tense
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: past tense

questions.onCorrect: An event such as `InventoryUpdated` records a fact, so its name is in the past tense. An imperative name makes readers expect a receiver that can refuse.

misconceptions.feedback: An imperative or present name reads as a request to one receiver. An event reports something that has already happened.
Nothing in an event is still to come. It records what is already true.

questions.prompt: A retry stored a deposit event twice, so a replay of the log gives too high a balance. Which fix keeps the log trustworthy?
hints: Replay applies every event it finds, so ask how it could recognise one it has met.
The fix should survive the next retry.

acceptedIdeas: Give each event an id, and let the consumer skip an id it has already applied
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Give each event an id, and let the consumer skip an id it has already applied

questions.onCorrect: An id lets the consumer apply each event once, however many times it arrives, so retries become safe.

choices.label: Delete one of the two events from the log by hand
Give each event an id, and let the consumer skip an id it has already applied
Stop retrying failed writes, so that no event is stored twice
Store the balance as well, and trust it over the log whenever they differ

misconceptions.feedback: The log is the record, and editing it by hand loses the trail. Duplicates will return with the next retry.
Without retries, a failed write loses an event, and the balance is wrong in the other direction.
Two sources of truth that can disagree make every rebuild a risk, and the log is meant to be the record.

questions.prompt: A refund flow must return money, restock the item and email the customer, and if the restock fails the return of money has to be undone. Which style suits it, and why?
hints: Ask who knows, at the moment the restock fails, that the money must be returned to the customer's card.
A flow with a few steps that rarely change favours the style in which one place holds the flow.

acceptedIdeas: Orchestration, since one place can run the steps in order and undo them on a failure
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Orchestration, since one place can run the steps in order and undo them on a failure

questions.onCorrect: A coordinator holds the whole flow, so a failure at one step can be handled where the other steps are known.

choices.label: Choreography, since every service can then react at its own pace
Orchestration, since one place can run the steps in order and undo them on a failure
Choreography, since a central service would be a single point that every flow depends on
Event sourcing, since it stores each refund step in a log

misconceptions.feedback: Each service reacts only to the event before it, so nobody sees the whole flow, and undoing the first step after a later failure has no owner.
That cost is real, but a flow of a few fixed steps that needs an undo gains more from one place that knows what happens next.
Event sourcing stores state as events. It does not coordinate services or undo a step.

questions.prompt:
A consumer reads messages with this function:

`import json`
`def read(msg):`
 `d = json.loads(msg)`
 `return d.get("qty", 1) * d["price"]`

What does `print(read('{"price": 4, "extra": true}'))` show?
hints: Find which keys the function actually reads.
Ask what `get` returns when a key is absent.

acceptedIdeas: 4, since `qty` defaults to 1 and `extra` is never looked at
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 4, since `qty` defaults to 1 and `extra` is never looked at

questions.onCorrect: Running it prints 4. The function reads two fields and supplies a default for one, so it tolerates both a missing optional field and an extra one.

choices.label: A `KeyError`, since the message has no `qty`
An error, since `extra` is not a field the function knows
0, since a missing `qty` counts as zero
4, since `qty` defaults to 1 and `extra` is never looked at

misconceptions.feedback: `get` returns the default 1 when the key is missing, so no error is raised.
The function reads only `qty` and `price`, and it never looks at other fields.
The default given to `get` is 1, so the price is multiplied by 1.

questions.prompt: A provider is renaming the response field `qty` to `quantity` with expand and contract, and five clients read `qty`. In what order do these steps happen?
hints: At every step each client must still have a name it can read.
The old name can be removed only after something shows that nobody reads it.

items: The provider sends both `qty` and `quantity`
Each client moves from `qty` to `quantity` at its own pace
The provider checks that no client reads `qty` any more
The provider stops sending `qty`

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The provider first sends both names, then each client migrates, then the provider confirms that none still reads qty, and only then stops sending it.

questions.onCorrect: Because the old name stays until the last client has moved, no step breaks a correct client, and the cost is a period in which the provider carries both names.

questions.prompt: A provider is planning seven changes to its API. Which are backwards compatible for existing clients that ignore fields they do not know, and which are breaking?
hints: Ask whether a correct existing client could fail after the change.
Changes that add leave the old uses alone, and changes that alter or remove do not.

items.label: Add a new endpoint
items.explanation: Existing clients never call it, so nothing they use changes.

items.label: Accept a new optional parameter in requests
items.explanation: Requests that omit it still work.

items.label: Add a field to a response
items.explanation: Clients that ignore unknown fields carry on as before.

items.label: Rename a response field
items.explanation: Every client that reads the old name now finds nothing.

items.label: Change a field from a number to a string
items.explanation: Clients that parse the number fail on the string.

items.label: Make an optional request field required
items.explanation: Every client that omits it is now rejected.

items.label: Tighten validation so that requests that used to pass are refused
items.explanation: Requests that used to be accepted now fail.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The new endpoint, the optional parameter and the added response field are compatible; the rename, the type change, the newly required field and the tighter validation are breaking.

questions.onCorrect: The safe changes add and do not alter, and any change that removes, renames, retypes or newly requires something can break a client that was correct before.

questions.prompt: A provider adds a field `discount` to a response. One client checks each response against a schema that lists the known fields and rejects any other. A second client reads only the fields it needs. What happens?
hints: Ask how each client treats a field it has never heard of.
Whether an addition is safe depends on how the consumers read.

acceptedIdeas: The strict client breaks and the other carries on, so safety depends on the reader
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The strict client breaks and the other carries on, so safety depends on the reader

questions.onCorrect: The strict client rejects the unknown field and the tolerant one ignores it, so even an addition is only as safe as the weakest reader.

choices.label: The strict client breaks and the other carries on, so safety depends on the reader
Both keep working, since adding a field never breaks a client that works
Both break, since the response no longer matches the version they were built for
Only the second client breaks, since it does not know of the new field

misconceptions.feedback: A client that rejects fields it does not know breaks on the new one, so an addition is safe only for readers that tolerate it.
The second client reads only what it needs and never meets the new field.
It does not need the new field, and it never looks at it. The strict client is the one that is troubled.

questions.prompt: A container diagram shows three boxes named Web, Service and DB, joined by arrows with no labels. A dashed box and a person-shaped icon appear with no explanation. Which single change helps a new reader most?
hints: Ask what a reader has to guess when they meet this diagram without its author.
Think about the three things the hygiene rules ask for: elements, arrows and shapes.

acceptedIdeas: Label every arrow, describe every box and add a key to the diagram
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Label every arrow, describe every box and add a key to the diagram

questions.onCorrect: Names, types, descriptions, arrow labels and a key mean the diagram can be read without its author present.

choices.label: Give each technology its own colour, so the boxes can be told apart
Add the classes inside each box, so that nothing is left to guess
Label every arrow, describe every box and add a key to the diagram
Draw the arrows thicker, so that the direction is easier to see

misconceptions.feedback: Colours need a key, and they say nothing about what a box is or what an arrow carries.
Classes belong to a lower level, and the diagram would mix levels and become harder to read.
The direction is not the trouble. A reader cannot tell what each arrow carries or what the shapes mean.

questions.prompt: On her first day a new developer needs to know which separate programs and data stores must be running on her machine. Which C4 level shows that?
hints: Ask which level opens the system into things that are started or stored.
A web app, an API and a database are all of one kind in C4.

acceptedIdeas: Containers, since each one is a separately runnable unit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Containers, since each one is a separately runnable unit

questions.onCorrect: A container is any separately runnable unit, including a database, so the container diagram lists what has to be running.

choices.label: System context, since it shows the system's users and neighbours
Components, since they show the inner parts of the system
Code, since classes show what each program is made of
Containers, since each one is a separately runnable unit

misconceptions.feedback: The context level treats the system as one box, so it does not say what runs inside it.
Components open up one container. She needs the runnable parts of the whole system first.
Classes do not say which programs or stores must be started.

questions.prompt: A team wants a diagram that shows on which machines, in which regions and behind which networks its containers run. Which supplementary C4 view shows that?
hints: Two supplementary views cover what the four levels leave out. One shows a scenario, and the other shows where things run.
The word for putting software onto machines names the view.

acceptedIdeas: deployment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: deployment

questions.onCorrect: A deployment view shows where the containers run, which a container diagram deliberately leaves out.

misconceptions.feedback: A dynamic view shows one scenario as a sequence of calls. It does not show where the containers run.
A container diagram shows what the runnable parts are and says very little about where they run.

questions.prompt: A matrix ranks option B first when performance has weight 0.5. At weight 0.7 for performance, option A ranks first. No score has changed. What should the team do?
hints: Ask what the scores describe and what the weights describe.
If a plausible change in the weights flips the winner, the weights are what the decision hangs on.

acceptedIdeas: Argue about the weights in the open, since the ranking depends on them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Argue about the weights in the open, since the ranking depends on them

questions.onCorrect: The scores describe the options and the weights describe what the team cares about, so a flip means the real argument is over the weights.

choices.label: Pick B, since the first weights chosen are the fair ones
Argue about the weights in the open, since the ranking depends on them
Hide the second ranking, since two answers would confuse the readers
Pick A, since weighting performance higher is always the safer choice

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing makes the first weights fairer. They were also chosen by a person, and the ranking has shown it depends on them.
The flip is the most useful result of the matrix. Hiding it also hides the assumption that decides the outcome.
No weight is always safer. The weights express what this team cares about, and the team has to decide that.

questions.prompt: A team records its decision to run its own PostgreSQL server instead of a hosted database. Which draft of the Consequences section follows Nygard's guidance?
hints: Consequences describe the situation after the decision is applied, including the costs.
Check which draft says what becomes harder as well as what becomes easier.

acceptedIdeas: We get full control over extensions and tuning, and we must run backups, upgrades and failover ourselves.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: We get full control over extensions and tuning, and we must run backups, upgrades and failover ourselves.

questions.onCorrect: A record that names the extra work as well as the control lets a later reader see the price that was accepted.

choices.label: The team compared hosted and self-run options in March, and the product's data must stay in its own region.
We will run our own PostgreSQL server and keep a copy of every backup on a second site.
We get full control over extensions and tuning, and we must run backups, upgrades and failover ourselves.
We get full control over extensions and tuning, and a lower monthly bill than a hosted service.

misconceptions.feedback: That is context, the forces behind the decision. Consequences describe what the team's situation becomes afterwards.
That is the decision, stated as a plan. Consequences describe what follows from it, good and bad.
It lists only the gains. Nygard asks for all the consequences, and what gets harder, such as the backups, belongs beside what gets easier.

questions.prompt: A team records that orders are stored in PostgreSQL. A year later it moves orders to a document store. In what order do these things happen to the records?
hints: A record is not accepted until the stakeholders agree to it.
The old record is only marked superseded once a later one exists to replace it.

items: The team writes the PostgreSQL record with the status proposed
The stakeholders agree, and the status becomes accepted
A new record chooses the document store and names the PostgreSQL record it replaces
The PostgreSQL record's status changes to superseded

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The PostgreSQL record is proposed, then accepted when the stakeholders agree. A later record chooses the document store and names the old one, and then the old record becomes superseded.

questions.onCorrect: The status lets a record be corrected without being lost, and the later record names the one it replaces so that both stay readable.

questions.prompt: A team writes the Decision section of a record about its order storage. Which version follows Nygard's guidance?
hints: The decision is stated in a full sentence in the active voice, starting "We will".
Reasons for the choice belong in another section.

acceptedIdeas: We will store orders in PostgreSQL, with one database for each service
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: We will store orders in PostgreSQL, with one database for each service

questions.onCorrect: A plain "We will" sentence is what a future developer finds first, and the reasons sit in the context and consequences.

choices.label: We will store orders in PostgreSQL, with one database for each service
Orders should probably go in a relational database, if that turns out to be possible
PostgreSQL, one database per service, for orders and their lines
PostgreSQL has better joins than the document stores we compared, so it won

misconceptions.feedback: It is hedged and passive, so a future reader cannot tell what was decided.
It is a list of fragments. Nygard asks for full sentences in the active voice.
That is the reasoning, and it belongs in the context. The decision is a plain statement of what was chosen.

questions.prompt: A pull request makes the domain package import the web framework. An accepted record says the domain must not do that. What should happen?
hints: Ask whether the change contradicts a record, and what the options are if it does.
A decision can be reversed, but the reversal should be visible.

acceptedIdeas: Revise the change, or write a new record that supersedes the old one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Revise the change, or write a new record that supersedes the old one

questions.onCorrect: Either the change gives way to the record, or a new record explains the reversal, and in both cases the reasons stay on the page.

choices.label: Merge it, since the code is the truth and the record is only history
Merge it, and edit the old record so that it quietly agrees with the code
Revise the change, or write a new record that supersedes the old one
Reject it without comment, since records can never be changed

misconceptions.feedback: A change that reverses a decision without saying so is the usual sign of drift. The reasons in the record are lost with it.
Rewriting the record hides that a decision was reversed and why. A new record that supersedes the old one keeps both readable.
Records can be superseded when the context changes. A reviewer should say which record the change contradicts.

questions.prompt: Module A is used by 3 other modules and uses 1. Module B is used by no module and uses 4. Which is easier to change safely, and why?
hints: Count how many modules would break if each of these changed.
A link into a module is a promise that others have relied on.

acceptedIdeas: B, since nothing depends on it, so a change breaks no other module
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: B, since nothing depends on it, so a change breaks no other module

questions.onCorrect: B has no dependents, so its instability is 1 and it can change freely, while A has an instability of 0.25 and should change rarely.

choices.label: B, since nothing depends on it, so a change breaks no other module
A, since it depends on only one module
A, since three modules rely on it and will notice any problem quickly
Both equally, since each has a few links

misconceptions.feedback: Having few outgoing links does not help when three modules depend on A. A change to A reaches all three.
Being noticed is not the same as being safe. A change that those three modules do not expect breaks them.
What counts is which way the links point. Incoming links make a module costly to change.

questions.prompt: A shortcut saved 6 hours and adds 1 hour to every later change. Repairing it would take 10 hours. The module will be retired after 4 more changes. What should the team do?
hints: Work out what the shortcut will still cost before the module is retired.
Compare that total with the cost of the repair.

acceptedIdeas: Leave it, since the 4 hours of interest are less than the 10-hour repair
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leave it, since the 4 hours of interest are less than the 10-hour repair

questions.onCorrect: Four more changes cost 4 hours of interest against 10 hours of repair, so the debt is cheaper to carry until the module is retired.

choices.label: Repair it now, since technical debt always grows if it is left
Repair half of it, since 5 hours splits the difference
Repair it, since the shortcut saved only 6 hours and the repair costs more
Leave it, since the 4 hours of interest are less than the 10-hour repair

misconceptions.feedback: The interest is 1 hour a change, and only 4 changes remain, so the debt cannot grow beyond 4 hours before the module is retired.
A half repair does not remove half of the interest in any useful way, and it still costs hours that the module will not repay.
What the shortcut saved is already spent. The decision compares the remaining interest with the cost of repair.

questions.prompt: A team must restructure an untested pricing function without changing what it does. In what order do they work?
hints: Nothing can be checked until the current behaviour has been recorded.
Each change is small, so a failing test points at it.

items: Run the function on sample orders and write tests that assert what it returns today
Make one small structural change, such as extracting a function
Run the tests and confirm that they still pass
Commit the change
Repeat with the next small change, running the tests after each

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The characterisation tests come first, then one small change is made, the tests are run and the change is committed, and the cycle repeats.

questions.onCorrect: The safety net is built first, and each small step is checked against it, so an accidental change in behaviour shows up at once.

questions.prompt: A company wants to replace a ten-year-old billing system. Plan A builds the new system over eighteen months and switches over on one weekend. Plan B puts a router in front and moves invoices first, then payments, then reports. Which plan do you advise, and why?
hints: Ask what the company has working, and what it can use, at the end of the first three months in each plan.
A migration is safest when it can be stopped or reversed at every step.

acceptedIdeas: Plan B, since it works at every stage and a slice can move back
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Plan B, since it works at every stage and a slice can move back

questions.onCorrect: Each slice moves when it is ready and can move back, and the old system is retired only when nothing is left on it.

choices.label: Plan A, since a clean break avoids running two systems at once
Plan B, since it works at every stage and a slice can move back
Plan A, since a router is one more thing that can fail
Plan B, but retire the old system as soon as invoices have moved

misconceptions.feedback: A big-bang rewrite delivers nothing until it is complete, and then replaces a working system in one step with no way back.
A router is a small price against eighteen months of work that cannot be tested in use.
The old system can be retired only when it has no work left, and payments and reports still run on it.

questions.prompt: A review finds the domain package importing the web framework in three new places, each added to save an hour. A record on layers says it must not. What should the team do to stop this recurring?
hints: Ask which check would catch the next import without anyone having to remember.
A record says why the boundary exists, and something else has to enforce it.

acceptedIdeas: Add a fitness function that fails the build on such an import, and keep the record
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Add a fitness function that fails the build on such an import, and keep the record

questions.onCorrect: The fitness function enforces the boundary on every build, and the record tells a reviewer why it exists.

choices.label: Ask reviewers to watch for it, since a rule is as good as the reviewers who remember it
Add a fitness function that fails the build on such an import, and keep the record
Remove the record, since the code no longer follows it
Rewrite the domain package, since it has eroded too far to repair

misconceptions.feedback: People forget under deadline, and a decision that nothing enforces is slowly worn away.
That makes the drift official and removes the reasons for the boundary.
Three imports can be removed one at a time. A rewrite is a large cost for a problem a check would catch.

flashcards.front: What is the shortest description of software architecture used in this course?
flashcards.back: Architecture is the set of decisions about structure that are costly to change later.

flashcards.front: A quality attribute scenario has how many parts?
flashcards.back: Six: source, stimulus, artefact, environment, response and response measure.

flashcards.front: Which part of a scenario holds the number a test compares against?
flashcards.back: The response measure, which is why it turns a wish into a requirement.

acceptedIdeas: response measure
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: response measure

flashcards.front: How many links join n modules when every module depends on every other?
flashcards.back: n × (n − 1) ÷ 2, so 6 modules have 15.

flashcards.front: What is feature envy?
flashcards.back: A method that uses another class's data more than its own, which suggests it belongs on that class.

flashcards.front: Why does a class that formats invoices and also sends email have low cohesion?
flashcards.back: It has two unrelated reasons to change, so a change to one risks the other.

flashcards.front: What is a leaky abstraction?
flashcards.back: An interface that exposes an implementation detail, so that callers come to depend on it.

flashcards.front: What did Parnas say a module should hide?
flashcards.back: A design decision that is difficult or likely to change, so that a change to it stays inside one module.

flashcards.front: What does a leading underscore on a Python name mean?
flashcards.back: It is a convention marking the name as internal, and the language does not enforce it.

flashcards.front: Which principle says code written for a base type must keep working when given a subtype?
flashcards.back: Liskov substitution: code written for the base type keeps working when given the subtype, so the subtype must honour the base type's behaviour.

acceptedIdeas: liskov substitution
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: liskov substitution

flashcards.front: Which four-letter acronym warns against building for needs you do not have yet?
flashcards.back: YAGNI, short for “you aren't gonna need it”, since the guessed need is often wrong and the code has to be kept anyway.

acceptedIdeas: yagni
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: yagni

flashcards.front: Why are the SOLID principles heuristics rather than laws?
flashcards.back: Applying them mechanically adds abstraction that can cost more in complexity than it saves.

flashcards.front: What is composition?
flashcards.back: Building behaviour by holding other objects and delegating to them, instead of inheriting from them.

flashcards.front: Three transports and three formats: how many subclasses does inheritance need for every pair?
flashcards.back: 3 × 3 = 9, against 3 + 3 = 6 parts with composition.

flashcards.front: In one sentence, when should you inherit and when should you compose?
flashcards.back: Inherit for a substitutable specialisation, and compose to reuse behaviour.

flashcards.front: Which pattern lets a subject notify subscribers of a change without knowing what they do?
flashcards.back: Observer: the subject holds a list and calls each subscriber in turn.

acceptedIdeas: observer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: observer

flashcards.front: How many patterns did the 1994 book Design Patterns describe?
flashcards.back: 23 patterns, by Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides.

flashcards.front: When is applying a pattern a mistake?
flashcards.back: When no problem exists yet, because the pattern then adds indirection without any benefit.

flashcards.front: What is ubiquitous language?
flashcards.back: One vocabulary shared by developers and domain experts, used in the conversation and in the code.

flashcards.front: What separates an entity from a value object?
flashcards.back: An entity is identified by an identity that persists as its data changes, while a value object is defined entirely by its data.

flashcards.front: What is the boundary called inside which a term has one meaning?
flashcards.back: A bounded context.

acceptedIdeas: bounded context
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: bounded context

flashcards.front: What is a seam?
flashcards.back: A place where behaviour can be replaced without editing the code, such as an argument that supplies a dependency.

flashcards.front: Which kind of test double returns canned answers?
flashcards.back: A stub returns canned answers, while a fake works in a small way and a mock records calls.

acceptedIdeas: stub
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: stub

flashcards.front: A rule allows entry when `age >= 18`. How many boundary cases does it need?
flashcards.back: Two: 17, which is refused, and 18, which is accepted.

flashcards.front: Which word names the interface the domain defines for something it needs?
flashcards.back: A port is the interface that the domain defines for something it needs or offers, which adapters implement or call.

acceptedIdeas: port
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: port

flashcards.front: Which rule says that source-code dependencies point inward, toward the domain?
flashcards.back: The dependency rule says that source-code dependencies point inward, toward the domain, and never outward to frameworks.

acceptedIdeas: dependency rule
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: dependency rule

flashcards.front: Why can a layered design still be tightly coupled?
flashcards.back: If everything depends on the data layer's shapes, a change to the database reaches every layer above it.

flashcards.front: Which style is one deployable unit with enforced module boundaries?
flashcards.back: A modular monolith.

acceptedIdeas: modular monolith
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: modular monolith

flashcards.front: Five services in a chain are each 99.9% available. What is the chain's availability, in percent, to one decimal place?
flashcards.back: 0.999 to the power 5 is 0.995, so 99.5%.

flashcards.front: Why do services that share one database table fail to be independent?
flashcards.back: A change to the table's schema must be agreed by every service that reads it, so they are coupled through the table.

flashcards.front: How does an event's name differ from a command's?
flashcards.back: An event is named in the past tense, such as OrderPlaced, and a command in the imperative, such as PlaceOrder.

flashcards.front: A store keeps every change as a record and rebuilds the state by replaying them. What is each stored change called?
flashcards.back: The sequence of events, with the state rebuilt by replaying them.

acceptedIdeas: events
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: events

flashcards.front: Why must a consumer of an event log be able to tell that it has already applied an event?
flashcards.back: Replay applies every event it finds, so a duplicate changes the result. An id on each event lets the consumer skip one it has seen.

flashcards.front: What is a breaking change?
flashcards.back: A change that makes a correct existing client fail, such as removing or renaming a field, changing a type, or tightening validation.

flashcards.front: Which technique adds the new form beside the old, moves clients across, and only then removes the old form?
flashcards.back: Expand and contract, done over three releases.

acceptedIdeas: expand and contract
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: expand and contract

flashcards.front: Why is adding a field not always safe?
flashcards.back: A strict consumer that rejects fields it does not know will fail when a new one appears.

flashcards.front: Name the four C4 levels from widest to narrowest.
flashcards.back: Context, containers, components, code.

acceptedIdeas: context, containers, components, code
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: context, containers, components, code

flashcards.front: Is a C4 container the same as a Docker container?
flashcards.back: No. A C4 container is any separately runnable unit, such as a web app, a mobile app or a database.

flashcards.front: What does a C4 container diagram leave out, and where does that go?
flashcards.back: Deployment detail such as clustering, load balancers and failover. A deployment view shows where the containers run.

flashcards.front: What five fields does an architecture decision record have?
flashcards.back: Title, status, context, decision, consequences.

acceptedIdeas: title, status, context, decision, consequences
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: title, status, context, decision, consequences

flashcards.front: What is a fitness function?
flashcards.back: An automated check that a chosen architectural property still holds, such as no domain module importing the web framework.

flashcards.front: A scores 8, 5, 6 with weights 0.5, 0.3, 0.2. What is the weighted total?
Which expression of Ca and Ce gives a module's instability?
flashcards.back: I = Ce / (Ca + Ce), where Ce counts outgoing dependencies and Ca counts incoming ones.

acceptedIdeas: Ce / (Ca + Ce)
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ce / (Ca + Ce)

flashcards.front: What is the strangler pattern?
flashcards.back: A facade routes requests to new code one slice at a time, until the old system has no work left and can be removed.

flashcards.front: Why write a characterisation test before refactoring untested code?
flashcards.back: It records what the code does today, so that an unintended change can be detected.
